articles.title: What Is the Meaning of Mystical Experience?
articles.text: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube What would it be like to wake up one day with the ability to greet the world with warmth, patience, grace, and affection? This is what happens to the main character in the Pulitzer Prize winner Ayad Akhtar’s magnificent new novel, The Radiance . It is a tale of spiritual transformation in which Akhtar gives a detailed description of our inner landscapes. David and Akhtar talk about what it’s like to see the world with new eyes, and how difficult it is to move from the head to the heart. The following is a transcript of the episode: David Brooks: Ayad Akhtar is one of America’s leading playwrights and writers. His plays, like The Disgraced , which won the Pulitzer Prize, and his earlier novels, including Homeland Elegies , often describe what it’s like to be a Muslim American in the post-9/11 era. His characters, Muslim and non-Muslim alike, are often coping with rage, pressure, resentments, hostility, a feeling of being judged. His new novel, The Radiance , is about a man whose spiritual state is transformed, who begins to radiate a glow which emerges from a kind of inner illumination. You could say he becomes one of those incandescent people you meet from time to time. I’m not exaggerating when I say it’s something of a masterpiece. The book brilliantly puts into words that most ineffable thing—spiritual sensations and experience. If you read it, which of course I recommend, you’ll be led on a tour through those deep inner places that most of us struggle to see and understand. When I started doing this podcast, I thought I’d have great conversations at an intellectual and emotional level that I feel comfortable with. But now, as I prepare to talk with Ayad, I feel like a person who’s about to jump off a high dive into a bottomless pool even though he can’t swim. I’m nervous and even a little afraid because I’m gonna talk to someone who knows about the realms I struggle to see and understand. I’m beginning to get the sense that this job is going to demand that I enlarge and deepen myself in ways that I hadn’t planned for but may end up doing me some good in the end. If you come along for the ride, I think the conversation will have the same effect on you. I’m David Brooks, and this is The Permanent Questions . Brooks: Ayad Akhtar, welcome to The Permanent Questions . Akhtar: Thank you, David. Brooks: On the cover of your book is a blurb by Abraham Verghese, who wrote The Covenant of Water and other things, and the blurb is: “Simply put, a work of genius.” And when I read that— Akhtar: I’m sorry. ( Laughs .) Brooks: —of course I wanted to kill you. But, I thought, Well, I’m a little suspicious. Maybe it’s just a friend . But this book, simply put, is a work of genius. I think it’s just gonna be one of the important books. You know, it’s been a few years since we’ve had a novel that was really a literary occasion. And I’d say this book is that literary occasion, in part because of the stuff we’ll talk about, but in part because we’ve lived in an era where so many spiritual poisons have been let loose by politics, by technology, by the general rancor. And here’s a book that takes spiritual life seriously and really lays out the inner world and describes a landscape of it. And I found that remarkable. And I have to say, I’m a little intimidated, because I try to think about the spiritual life, but it’s all a little fuzzy down there. I think one of the things the book did for me was give me words to describe some of the things you vaguely feel, and also just to think, Well, how does spiritual life develop and grow? And so I guess, my first simple question is: Describe the premise and the concept of the novel. Akhtar: So a writer who has my name and many of the facts of my life—which is something I’m sure we’ll talk a little bit about—leaves the city after writing a previous book in which he had done the same thing, given the narrator his name and many of the facts of his life, and moves to the country. And after being there for a while, is out on a country road on a bike and gets hit by a pickup truck from behind, thrown into a grove of trees, and wakes up in a hospital after a coma about 36 hours later. And as he awakens into himself, something’s changed. There’s a luminosity and a silence that is the ground of his experience. And then that experience seems to deepen and get more complex over the subsequent eight months. And the book basically tracks that eight-month period. Simultaneously to this, he also has a friend who is teaching at a local college where he is asked to teach as well for a semester. And so the ongoing political divisions on campus, as well as within the local rural community, play a significant role as our narrator experiences what some friend of mine once called, in reading it, something like a “beatitude” or a “state of grace.” Brooks: He’s luminous, he’s incandescent, and he’s having a great time. And the first thing I love about his state of consciousness is that it’s about perception. And the very beginning of the book, before you even get to the chapters, the sentence is: “This is a record of altered perceptions.” Akhtar: Yeah. Brooks: And what I like about that is, we used to think perception, the act of seeing the world, was this passive thing. You open your eyes, the world floods in, and you record it the way an old camera would record light. We now know from neuroscience that’s not the way it happens. But even more, I think we’ve learned that—it used to be, you thought, Well, you see the world, and then you think about the world, and then you act on the world . And we used to think the action is in the middle. It’s in the thinking. But in my view, it’s in the perception. It’s in the seeing and the way you see and the quality of attention. And that quality of attention you bring to the world determines what you see in the world. If you’re distrustful, you’re gonna see threat, and if you’re loving, you’re gonna see people doing the best they can. This is where I’m hoping to walk you into. Mystics have always paid a lot of attention to perception. And the one I know best is Simone Weil, who was a French mystic in World War II and said that attention is the ultimate form of generosity. Your primary form of morality is what kind of attention you bring to the world. And one of her followers, Iris Murdoch, who was a novelist and a philosopher, says our goal is to cast a just and loving attention on others. And so what you see with this character is a man learning to attend the world in a radically different way than he used to. Akhtar: Well, I think that’s fascinating the way you laid it out. I think that’s right. I think in thinking about the book, there was a difference between rendering new experiences and rendering processes that were the result of something that was experiencing itself. That is to say, a change of the one who is experiencing. So it’s not just states. There’s also a moral dimension to the change that he doesn’t really understand. He’s not trying to be a good person. He’s just trying to understand what’s happened and spends a fair amount of time at the doctor’s office trying to figure out what’s going on. Brooks: Trying to be a good person—there’s all sorts of ways to do that. People think, Well, you build up these muscles. I got a courage muscle. I got an honesty muscle. I’m gonna build my muscle, and I’ll be a good person . But I don’t think that’s the way morality works. It’s the quality of love you bring to your perception of the world. Akhtar: I think there is something about the self-evident nature of relating to the world in a certain way. Emerson has a beautiful thing that he says, that virtue is the secret pillar that holds up the world. Which, in a way, is a way of saying that virtue is an efficient cause—that the best way to get something done is to be virtuous. It may not be the quickest way, but it might be the best way in the end. These are not ideas that he’s trying to follow. They’re just experiences, and he approaches those experiences with just as much skepticism as pleasure. Because keeping that question alive—about what is happening, why does this matter, what are the implications of it?—felt to me important for a reader today. Brooks: So for him, it comes as this weird gift as the product of a nearly fatal accident. Akhtar: As it happened, by the way, for Montaigne. Montaigne was thrown from a horse and spent the next four days in a kind of beatitude that totally transformed his life. Brooks: The Montaigne story, I’ve always loved it, because he was worried about how to die, and then this happens to him, and he records his own body as he’s near death having had this accident. And he says, “Oh, the body knows how to die. I don’t have to worry about this anymore.” My father passed away about three or four months ago. He was the only person I’ve ever walked to death. And I was like, “Yeah, the body really knows what to do.” That was a great comfort to me. Now, you have a piece forthcoming in The Atlantic , which is not really an excerpt from the book, but it’s in the neighborhood of the book. It’s sort of a nonfiction piece, and it’s really more about you directly. You didn’t have an accident, but you had a process. And so describe that. Akhtar: In college, I started to have a very alarming experience that I couldn’t ignore, that there was some sort of a hole opening up inside me, and it was a curiously physical sensation. It was very, very concrete. My parents are both doctors, so I spent some time trying to figure out what the medical genesis of this was and could not get any clarity on that. My mom sent me to a psychoanalyst, who was more interested in my sex life than any kind of hole that might be opening up inside me. But I started to pay attention to this experience. And the psychoanalytic sessions got me interested in Freud. So I started reading Freud, and I read The Interpretation of Dreams and started to have some very, very vivid dreams and started paying attention to my dreams. And then had a mentor who also paid attention to her dreams and taught me a little bit how to pay attention to my dreams. And close attention to my dreams for many years I think opened up some different kind of space in my psyche, in my being, in my life, and led me down a path where I started to spend more and more time focused inwardly. We might call it meditation. But I’m not sure folks would recognize what I was doing as meditation. And I think that inner attention got me focused on a level or a layer of subtle experience we’re always having. And the more attention I brought to it—just as with dreams, the more focus I spent writing my dreams down, the more vivid and more dreams I had. At one point, I was waking up every 45 minutes to write my dreams down. This lasted two years. I literally have thousands and thousands of written dreams. But similarly, with this subtle layer of experience, the more attention I paid to it, the more it seemed to open up. So similarly in the book, as the writer is writing about this experience, it seems to somehow deepen it. Brooks: The sense of a hole. Akhtar: Yeah. Brooks: Now, I have a sense of a shallowness sometimes, like I’m just living on the surface. And I sometimes don’t know how to do what you just described, which is look inside. And you did it through dreams because dreams opened up different states of knowing, I guess? Akhtar: I mean, to quote something out of your own idiom, David, I think the need created an intense desire. I was a young person with a real sense that something was wrong. I’m not really going into full detail as I do in the essay about just how bad the experience was. It felt clear to me that I might not survive, that I would do something that would hurt me or hurt somebody else, or I might kill myself. So I think the experience was not just in a disembodied hole. The experience was all-consuming. When I read Thomas Merton’s [The] Seven Storey Mountain , I remember sort of recognizing in the spiritual crisis that he had at Cambridge and Columbia some aspects of what I was experiencing. For me, a solution could not be to go to a monastery or go to the church. I had lost my religious faith, and restoration of my religious faith was not gonna solve the problem. I had to somehow be attentive to the experience I was having and to trust. I don’t know why I had the trust that if I was, that something would emerge from that, some orientation would emerge from that that would help. And it did, it took a long time, and it’s one that I wanted to convey in the book, but I needed a more truncated and more dramatically impactful way to do so. Brooks: One of the things that strikes me is your instinct when you feel this void is not to go to psychology. Akhtar: I tried. Brooks: Oh, you did try. I mean, the Freud. Akhtar: My mom sent me to a psychiatrist. Brooks: But I have a friend who suffers severely from depression. He’s written about this, so it’s not a secret. He gets institutionalized from time to time, and the psychologist will not go to—he says, “My problem is spiritual. You don’t understand. It’s not psychological. It’s not my mom, or something like that.” And they can’t go there. Akhtar: Look, at the root of the word psychology is psyche , and psyche in Greek means “soul.” Modern psychology is burying the lede. We are concerned with issues of the soul, but that’s a word that we can’t really use anymore, and I get why we can’t use it. And part of the project of the book, and part of the project of this essay, was to try to find a language that was secular, for inner experience, that defies the secular frame and what it would mean to be paying a certain kind of attention to that experience. I think there are psychiatrists or psychologists who do understand this, and there is one in the book, actually. She has an openness to some of this stuff. The importance of it is not necessarily that we land on a model that is right, but we land on a model that’s useful to the one who is undergoing whatever process they’re undergoing. Brooks: When you gradually turned the corner, was there a moment, or was it this process of dream analysis? And then did you experience the radiance that the character in the book experiences? Akhtar: As for whether I experienced what the writer experiences in that book: Well, I couldn’t have written it if I hadn’t. ( Laughs .) But I certainly am giving it shapes that it doesn’t have in my life. Because even though he has my name and many of the facts of my life, we are not the same person. Brooks: I started writing down—because all spiritual experiences are ineffable. They’re hard to describe. And so I started—because I was so fascinated by how you did it—writing down all the different phrases you used to describe this state. You know, things like “a sublime burning calm,” “inner silence,” “effortless patience,” “a disembodied halo of self-awareness,” “a visionary tenderness.” And one of the things I think they all capture, you all sort of are getting closer to that state. Akhtar: A state which is always different. Brooks: What do you mean by that? Akhtar: Plato has this wonderful idea that we are caught between. We are in the metaxy. We live between the forms and the matter. And when we, in Plato’s terms, rise to the real, we’re not always rising to the same place. There’s different configurations. And so some of those states that he’s experiencing are more inflected by emotional tenderness, some by a certain kind of brilliancy of vision and clarity. Each of the experiences phenomenologically is a soul experience, and to have all of those experiences at the same time, I don’t really know how I would give language to that. Brooks: But they are in a movement. Akhtar: They are. Brooks: You have a quote from Dostoyevsky who writes, “An abnormal intensity if minute of sensation remembered and analyzed afterwards in health turns out to be the acme of harmony and beauty and fires the feeling unknown and undivided until then of completeness, of proportion, of reconciliation, of ecstatic devotional merging of the highest synthesis of life.” Akhtar: Yeah. Beautiful. Brooks: That’s a beautiful description. One of my favorite descriptions of joy comes from Zadie Smith. I read this somewhere, and she was out at a nightclub in 1999. It’s crowded and her feet hurt, and she can’t find her purse, and suddenly a song from the group A Tribe Called Quest comes on the sound system, and some stranger, a guy she doesn’t know, grabs her. He pulls her onto the dance floor and he says to her, “Are you feeling it? Are you feeling it?” She says, “I am. I am.” And she says, “Our heads exploded, and we gave ourself up to joy.” I’ve always loved that description of these highest states of transcendent beauty. I don’t know if you’re prone to those, but they’re delicious when they happen. Akhtar: Well, he certainly is. Another experience that he’s having in the book, which is an unusual one but one that’s reported by a lot of traditions, is that he starts to experience the localization of his consciousness or his awareness not in the head, but in the heart. That’s what I hear in Zadie’s description, that somehow the head explodes. That somehow the localization in the mind changes. You’re no longer just in your mind or even in your mind. Brooks: I don’t know if you share this as part of a central feature of your life, but my parents were academics. We grew up with a lot of books. So I’ve spent most of my life trying to move from my head about 18 inches down to my heart. That’s been my whole life, with some success and some failures. And you have a phrase, you refer to it as “the curious seeing with my chest.” Have you gone through the same struggle against overintellectualization? Ayad Akhtar: For sure. I had a wonderful mentor, remarkable mentor, Jerzy Grotowski, a Polish theater director of some renown. Most famously, I think for people, My Dinner With Andre is largely based on Andre’s experiences in a Polish forest with Jerzy Grotowski. So I worked with him in my early 20s, and I remember almost the first day that we started working together, he said, “You’re not gonna read. You’re gonna stop reading. That’s it. No more reading for you.” I said, “Why?” He said, “Because you think too much. We need to get you into your body. I need you to be operating from a different part of yourself.” So I basically didn’t read for eight months. It was an interesting experience. The work was very physical and very vocal, and so not having that escape hatch to try to figure out what something meant or the defense of why it was okay I wasn’t able to do something—all of that still going on, but it was not as prevalent because I wasn’t spending the evenings when I was back home trying to sort it through by reading, which is something I’ve always done. But then I went back to reading. ( Laughs .) Brooks: Well, clearly, because you can’t write if you don’t read. John Stuart Mill was raised by his father, who was a big utilitarian, and his father’s friend Jeremy Bentham, and they just fed the kid books. He could read Greek when he was 3. He was incredible. And then he has a complete mental breakdown when he’s 20. And he realizes that an overemphasis on reading and analysis wears away feeling, and he finally recovers when he discovers poets—Wordsworth and Coleridge and those kind of guys. And that’s been a central problem with my own life. I sometimes worry that—career as a journalist and writer—I’m always on lecture mode, even to myself. Which I think is a way of making yourself unavailable for the resonance that you’re talking about, the falling into the deeper registers, because the voice is going, the voice, the voice. But when you need to quiet— Akhtar: Well, I have a practice. And the practice is about focus, inward focus, and the points of focus can change depending on how the practice is evolving. I’ve done all different kinds of stuff over 30 years, and so I’ve accumulated a—Laurence Olivier once said about building a performance that rehearsal was all about figuring out what buttons he needed to push. And the performance was just about pushing those buttons. So I’ve got a lot of buttons that I’ve accumulated. And I just figure out what buttons I need to push on any given day. As long as I have time to do it. And I think to me, that’s what I’ve discovered is that it really is about application of will in time. Commitment. And if I do it regularly, then sometimes I feel like I can have a more steady movement of the head to the heart, to use your language, or to quiet the mind or whatever it may be. And if I don’t do it, then that doesn’t happen. Brooks: And what exactly are you doing when you say you’re pushing the buttons? Akhtar: It’s so elaborate and so specific. A lot of what’s going on in the book is really me sharing various buttons. Different kinds of inner focus and seeing, focuses on different parts of the body, focus on different kinds of thoughts. Ibn Arabi, the great Sufi mystic visionary, talks about the higher use of the imagination, that the imagination is actually a tool to get us to the real. As Dante: Heaven is the “high fantasy.” Or Blake will use the imagination to approach some higher way of seeing. So similarly with Ibn Arabi, just the judicious use of the imagination can create states of absorption. Brooks: I think you can slip into—in journalism or whatever job people are in, finance—prosaic modes of consciousness that make this really hard. Akhtar: That’s right. Brooks: And I noticed when I first started praying, I was editing it. It was like, Oh, this prayer is so repetitive. It lacks coherence . And I remember once I was at a service, and the pastor asked us to pray for deaths in Syria, and we gathered with groups of three, and we’re supposed to pray, beseeching God to help those who were suffering in Syria. And I said, “Lord, please help pass UN Resolution 242, to provide safe zones for the—” I prayed an op-ed piece, basically. And I look back on that, it’s like, I suck at prayer. Would you say you—obviously you don’t believe in God—but something like that? Akhtar: It’s not that I don’t believe in God; it’s just I don’t see the utility of engaging in belief as a way of addressing my experience. Emerson has this wonderful—I’ve quoted Emerson a bunch just because I read him so much, and I know that there’s mind share between us around Emerson. I think Emerson once described prayer as a disease of the will. I think he means a certain kind of prayer—prayer for commodities, whether those commodities are intangible or tangible. And there’s maybe a different order of prayer that I can resonate with. I don’t necessarily pray, but I can resonate that it’s a different order of attention, a different kind of focus. But I think, if I do that regularly, if I build it into my life and I’m loyal to it, I get a good benefit, and if I don’t, then I don’t get the benefit. Brooks: When I came to faith, I was shocked at what faith was, and that I used to think it was about belief. You had to believe certain propositions. And, of course, it is about belief. It’s not totally void of belief. But I experienced it more as a longing than as a set of beliefs. Dorothy Day, my heroine, wrote a book called The Long Loneliness , and by loneliness, she did not mean solitude. She meant her longing for God. And one of the beautiful moments in her life comes at the end, where she’s asked by Robert Coles—she wrote this memoir, Long Loneliness , when she was young—and at the end of her life, she was asked, “Did you ever think of writing another one the rest of your life?” And Dorothy Day, for those who don’t know, was a woman who not only served the poor, but lived amongst the poor, a life of selfless love. And so she said to Coles, “I thought about writing a memoir, and so I got a legal pad and I wrote ‘A Life Remembered by Dorothy Day.’” And she said, “And I sat there, and I sat there, and I sat there, and I thought of the Lord and His visit to us those many centuries ago, and I was just grateful to have had Him on my mind all that time.” What’s so entrancing for me is that it’s serenity. Somehow she’s reached that spot of serenity, a simple serenity that the voices stop. So it’s a beautiful practice that she had to live through her whole life to get to that spot. Akhtar: Grotowski used to tell this story. We were translating something together. I spent a great deal of time with him in one period, and he told me this story on a couple of occasions. It was a kind of a technical story, trying to convey some technique to me about something. There’s a Hindu parable in which an aspirant goes to God and says to God, “I love you so much, God. You know how much I love you.” God says, “Oh yeah, you love me a lot.” And he says, “So how many lifetimes is it gonna take for me to get out of this birth and re-death and all this stuff?” And God says, “Well, you love me a lot. Seven. It’s gonna take you seven.” So he says, “Okay, all right, seven. So if I hated you, how many more would it take?” God says, “Well, if you really hated me, it would take you three.” The guy says, “What are you talking about?” Says, “If you really hated me, you’d think about me more.” And it was Grotowski’s way of conveying to me that really what mattered was intensity and application. And not so much intention or the moral valences around the intention. It’s a challenging proposition to think that you could experience something like a radiance without being committed to being a good person. But certainly that narrator is not necessarily committed to being a good person or a bad person. He’s just living the consequences of this grace. Brooks: I’m gonna pick up on that intentionality, the yearning which I was talking about. One of the things we tend to do in our society is we try to define human beings by what separates us from the other animals. We come, starting in Plato and up to the present day—reason. Reason is what distinguishes us from the animals. And I think that’s not true, but I was struck— Akhtar: You think it’s not true because you think animals also have a degree of reason? Brooks: I think that’s not what centrally defines us. I think your desires, your yearnings are telling you where you’re gonna go, where you’re gonna devote your energy. Reason is there to help you figure out how to get there. So it’s downstream, and emotions are there to tell you if you’re getting closer or further from where you wanna go. The part of the brain that really is most important to us is not the one that distinguishes us from the animals; it’s the one we share with the animals. Which is that longing, that yearning which comes from the rewards. Akhtar: And fear. Brooks: And fear. Absolutely. So that helps me think through where I want the center of my conception of myself to be. Akhtar: Which is? Brooks: Which is the stuff that doesn’t get measured on an SAT score. Akhtar: And it’s measured how, if at all? Brooks: I think it’s measured by sanctification and degradation, a feeling. There’s a line in C. S. Lewis that there’s some piece at the core inside of yourself, and every act you do turns that little core piece inside of yourself into something a little more holy or a little more profane. Akhtar: What does it mean for you for it to be more holy? What is the phenomenological experience of that? What does it actually feel like? If you had to give language to it. Brooks: This is why I’m not you. I have a friend who lived in India, and he said, “What I liked about it, in India, everything was on a vertical axis as well as a horizontal axis.” So you are having a moment of beauty, spiritual beauty. It feels like beauty. And more like a swelling out of the heart. That’s how it would feel. And I think of the moments in my life where I experienced the greatest sense of spiritual peace and joy, like the Zadie Smith story. One of mine was—I was pulling into my home. My kids were little back in those days, and we lived in the suburbs. We had a driveway that spun around the side of the house, so I could see into the backyard. My kids had one of those little balls that you get at the supermarket, and they were kicking it up in the air. I just sat there in my car looking through the windshield at my three kids tumbling over each other and laughing. I just sat there, and I had a swelling. Tears come to your eyes. It’s something touching you. I think I would call it—and I wanna return to this word you’ve used a couple times—a swelling of the soul. And now in your Atlantic piece, and I think in the book too, you’re uncomfortable with the word soul . I think you at one point call it an anachronistic concept. And yet you use it. Akhtar: Well, I’ve learned from Shakespeare that the best way to assert a meaning is to negate it with equal force. Any time a reader feels that you’re aligned with one thing against another, they naturally array themselves against you. So the way to create space for them to have freedom is to assert both poles with equal conviction. So the book, obviously—and I in my own intellectual life and with myself—because I notice that that tendentiousness is something that my own cognition partakes in, that if I’m too aligned with some particular thing, there’s some other part of me that begins to bark, Well, you didn’t think about it like this . So being equally committed to both orientations is a way to have more freedom. And it’s also a way to have the reader make up their own mind, if you will. Brooks: Is this a literary device or a personal reality for you? Akhtar: What’s the difference? All the great traditions—and certainly the Kabbalistic tradition is very, very clear about this, that reality is composed of oppositions and that you can’t have one thing without its opposite. That’s the warp and woof of everything. So I think that the extent to which language reflects that deeper truth, it is probably reflecting it in a literary form. And for me, Shakespeare is the one I spend the most time reading. I was reading him this morning just to try to get—he’s like Mozart for babies’ brains for me. It just kinda wakes me up a little bit. I get a lot of lessons from reading him, and that’s the big one. Brooks: Robert Maynard Hutchins wrote probably in the ’40s or ’50s. He was president of the University of Chicago. And he said there’s an eternal great conversation that we’ve been having as humans for thousands and thousands of years. And it’s between fitting in and standing out. Between individualism and belonging, between freedom and equality, between all the dialectics of life. And his point was these questions never end. You never get to a resting spot. It’s just you’re looking for the thing that’ll work at that moment. Akhtar: I think the pieties of any given cultural moment are fueled by the illusion that there is a resting place in that conversation. Brooks: Now, I wanna come back to the soul, because one of the really high watermarks of this book is a scene with Allan Bloom, who I knew at the University of Chicago. I was never part of the cult. He was a philosopher, and he wrote a great translation of The Republic , which I think is still read today. The narrator in the book is in love, and we’re gonna get into this, with a woman named Lucy. Lucy’s a brilliant woman, and she’s with Allan Bloom at the moment he tells her what a soul is. If you could walk us through that scene. Akhtar: I did a lot of research on Bloom for this book and that era at the University of Chicago, where Lucy was an undergraduate. One thing that many of his students who kept faith with Bloom’s teaching over the course of their years, whether as teachers or as people in their lives, kept referring to was this sense that somehow when he talked about the soul, you had a feeling—even though you couldn’t define it and he never really defined it—that you all knew what you were talking about. Which is a fascinating proposition. In this scene, young Lucy, who’s 22 years or 21 years old, is in his class, and she has been sitting in back because there’s never any chairs. And she shows up late because she’s got a class across campus. She comes down to the bottom of the auditorium after class and after all the courtiers have kissed the ring and left, and asks the great Allan Bloom, “You talked about a soul in today’s lecture. What exactly do you mean by a soul?” He then proceeds to ask her to close her eyes. He talks her through a bunch of questions, and she answers, and he responds, and she answers, and finally lands on an experience that she articulates in her own language that he then reflects back to her as a definition of the soul. She even says, “I’m not sure what this proved, and yet somehow everything was different, that my contact with whatever it was I had been inquiring about enlivened me.” So that’s the scene. Brooks: And then she comes to the belief the soul is the first mover. Akhtar: Well, it’s Plato. The soul is that which moves but is not moved by anything. You move your arm, you’re moving it. So what in us is always moving, but we’re not moving it? That’s what she connects with. Brooks: I would say something was lost and gained when we lost the concept of soul in public conversation. It’s true, vast majorities of Americans believe they have souls. But in most public culture, we just don’t talk about it. Akhtar: It’s discredited. Brooks: But I think it’s very hard to understand oneself without this concept of a soul. Akhtar: I think subjectivity is discredited. I think subjectivity is embraced as a radically individualist, totally relativistic idea or notion. I think the possibility there might be subjective facts is something that we are not equipped, intellectually, as a culture to grapple with. That’s what I’m suggesting by saying I think we need to have a conversation about things like the soul, even if we are gonna put them in quotes, because I think there’s a whole order of our experience, maybe the most important order of all of our experience, that we’re not actually having a conversation about. Brooks: Completely agree. Let’s talk about the care and feeding of the soul. I’m gonna insist on this word. How to enlarge the soul. Or how to purify or, I don’t know, make it more what it should be—let’s put it that way. So not to prejudge. There are different philosophies of how you purify your inner state. And one of them is self-emptying. You renounce desire; the Stoics had this belief in apathy. You just achieve tranquility. And there’s a lot of that in Eastern mysticism. And so you renounce the self, you take yourself out of the way, and you’re just quiet. Akhtar: That’d be great if I could do it, but I can’t do that. Brooks: I can’t do that either. Maybe by default, I’ve gone to another way of feeding the soul, which is—another of my heroes is Gregory of Nyssa, who was an early Church father and living in, I think it was what is now present-day Turkey. He was surrounded by Greek philosophies that had the idea that happiness is rest. You work hard, you achieve your goals, and you just rest and you can relax. That’s what happiness is. And he was like: My main goal in life is to know and understand and love God perfectly. But if I could do that perfectly, that would imply that God is finite, which He is not. Therefore, rest cannot be happiness. There must be something else. He has a sermon on—there are a lot of sermons on the Song of Songs. This is the sexy part of the Bible. The bridesmaid is chasing her beloved, and he withdraws, and she chases. With each chase and withdrawal, there’s an encounter. Each time, her love is more deep and her experience is more soaring. And so Gregory says, “No, it’s not in rest; it’s in pursuit.” That, to me, makes sense. It’s when I fall in love with something, and then something outside touches something inside and sets off an explosion, and I’m in pursuit of that thing. I think that’s when my soul is happiest. Akhtar: When you can trust your desire. What I would say to that, and what I think I tried to use the book to explore and for myself, was that attention to a certain kind of experience, attention to a certain subtle coursing continuity in my awareness, began to deepen and open into different terrains. And that exploration—maybe a kind of pursuit that you’re talking about—was not activated by a sense of longing or desire, in my case, but more activated by a curiosity. So I think we’re in the same ballpark. Brooks: Yeah, curiosity is a form of longing and desire. It’s a desire for understanding and clarity. Akhtar: Aristotle has it—we are defined as creatures, as the creatures who wish to know. So being in pursuit of knowledge is a different way I read what Gregory is talking about. Brooks: I think that’s right, though the longing to know can sometimes be a very weak passion in a lot of people. Akhtar: Well, there’s two words for “know” in French. One is savoir and one is connaître . And savoir is to “know about.” And connaître is to “know.” And one might be oriented toward an objective understanding of something, and the other a subjective understanding. Brooks: In the Bible “to know” obviously, famously, can mean to love, it can mean to have sex with, it can mean to enter into a covenant with. It’s a whole-body experience. And maybe in the Enlightenment or somewhere else, we divided that, and that division did great injury to how we understand ourselves, because it allowed— Akhtar: It created the modern world. Brooks: It did do that. Akhtar: We could go back to Descartes and say Descartes had a similar night of not being able to sleep and then decided to create this world that we now live in. And so there’s obviously been benefits, but we’ve lost a lot by not allowing that kind of knowledge, which again, is what I’m trying to focus on. It’s a knowledge that—I don’t know what it means. I just know that I’m experiencing it. Brooks: There’s a lot of love in the book, which I liked, and one of the most interesting relationships in the book is for the narrator with this woman, Lucy, who was the University of Chicago—lady we’ve been talking about. Akhtar: Who becomes a professor later. Brooks: And it’s literally Platonic love. So describe that love he has for her. Because he is pursuing her and fascinated by her and amazed by her, and she, by the way, has a wonderful marriage, which he does not wanna interfere with. Akhtar: I’ve had some extraordinary mentors in my life, and a number of the most important mentors have been women and have taught me about so much. And I resonate particularly—as we said earlier, there’s a lot of Plato in the book, and there’s a lot of Phaedrus in the book, one of the dialogues. And something else that there’s a lot of which I don’t talk about is the Symposium . In the Symposium , Socrates tells a story about how he learned about love and that there was an older woman who mentored him named Diotima. So Lucy’s a bit of that kind of a figure. Somebody who really has an understanding of eros in the higher sense of the word. What would it mean to relate to eros not out of a desire to possess, but to be animated by the aliveness in knowledge? So anyway, very high-minded, but I try to give it some juice in the book. David Brooks: C. S. Lewis, in his book The Four Loves , makes the distinction between “Need-love” and “Gift-love,” and Need-love proceeds out of a void, and it’s the desire to possess, to control. And Gift-love just flows out of a blessing. Akhtar: In Plato, this proposition in the Symposium is basically that love has a ladder, that you learn love in one form, and if you’re open to it, it leads to another kind of love, which then leads to another kind of love. It maybe starts with the body, but it elevates out of the body into some place higher. So, similarly, the book is exploring the possibility of what it would mean in a secular age to be related to your own experience and the experience of the world, not through a kind of materialist separation or wanting to accomplish or desire, but really just being attentive to the aliveness of that experience. Brooks: Now I’m presuming, and it’s really through your writing, you’ve had these numinous experiences. Have you had transcendent mountaintop experiences that William James used to write about, or that sort of thing? Akhtar: As time has gone on, over 30 years of various kinds of investigation and practice, I’ve had lots of different experiences. And I think more and more the experience that’s the most valuable to me is a kind of continuity of connectedness in the everyday, and feels to me more and more a better definition of the transcendent than some of the wild, dynamic, knock-your-socks-off experiences that I may have had, and that the narrator certainly does have in the book. Brooks: So connected to experience, that’s like, I am in the world . Akhtar: Connected to the continuity. There’s a continuity between us. Continuity with my ancestors. All of that stuff. That it’s here, it’s with us now. So being connected to that in a lived sense without self-consciousness That to me feels like a better definition of the transcendent. Brooks: I get that. Way before I had any faith, I had this sense of what you might call historical ecstasy. The moment of touching something or being someplace, like Chartres Cathedral or Gettysburg Battlefield, where the procession of people who’ve been there has left a residue. I was once at a home that was purported to be the home of Mary, outside of Ephesus in Turkey. I don’t know if Mary ever lived there, but centuries of prayers and mourners move through that space, and something is emanating from it, a sensation of the procession. I don’t know if I’m correctly interpreting what you’re describing. Akhtar: That’s certainly a version of what I’m talking about. I think what I’m talking about is even more prosaic. But yes. And by the way, the book does end in Chartres, interestingly. Brooks: I noticed that. Now, you have quoted Thomas Merton, and people like that, Augustine. Meister Eckhart comes up. A lot of your spiritual companions or guides, they took this, and they took it to religion. You accompany them part of the way, but you don’t take it to where they took it, which was the Bible or the Quran. Now, is that just: “I just don’t feel that. It just doesn’t feel authentic to me,” or have there been advantages and disadvantages to this spiritual sense that’s not tied to an institutionalized religion? Ayad Akhtar: It’s such a beautiful and cutting question. I don’t know. I think I’m trying to live by an empirical ethic, an ethos of being attentive to my experience, being attentive to those who’ve written about their experiences, trying to accumulate whatever wisdom over time that I can, recognizing that they are making connections both which I value and others which I don’t understand. I don’t wanna take anything on faith because to me, faith is not about an object. It’s about an orientation. I think I put it in The Atlantic essay—it is a living form of relationship with the unknown. That feels like its own worthy form of knowledge, to be in living relationship to the unknown. And not for it to have a name, because the name can sometimes get in the way of the practice. Doctrines are often things that were once practices that have now been turned into meanings. Now we consume them as meanings, but we have lost connection to the practice that led to some experience. I think mystics in general are focused on experience. And so maybe I just share that kind of granular phenomenological interest in experience itself. And I’m much more interested in that than I am in what it means. Because I’m not gonna get any kind of clarity about what it means. I may get clarity in a moment. But as the brain scans of nuns and Tibetan monks tell us—they are having very similar brain scans, but the language they use to report what their experience is is almost opposing: “union with Christ” or “emptiness.” So what does it matter what the concept is unless the concept is helping to activate technically? Does that make sense? Brooks: It does. And I’m not judging here or comparing. We’ve had two different experiences of this. Akhtar: Yours might be better. When I said it was a cutting question, I think that what my orientation lacks, which is important, is community. Because I’m a renegade out there on my own. I’ve never really talked much about this stuff. I’ve alluded to it a couple of times in interviews, but I’ve kept to myself about it, because it’s been an investigatory thing. It’s my pursuit. So I don’t have it to share with other people, which maybe suits me fine as a writer and as an observer and as an outsider, and maybe that’s my life choice, but I think it does deprive me of community. Brooks: Shiva, say, the Jewish mourning ritual, is a beautiful, very spiritually and intellectually very sophisticated way to handle grief. It also gives everybody in the congregation—they know what to do. Everyone knows exactly what to do. And I would say religion has provided me with a broader sensation, at least the way I process spiritual experiences. I was having one of these numinous experiences in Colorado. I was on the top of a mountain by a lake. And because I’m me—and even I was not a big believer then, I was still wandering in those days—I brought up a book called The Valley of Vision , which is a collection of Puritan prayers. I happened to open it when I’m having this very moving and beautiful experience. And the first prayer is a very famous one: “Lord, high and holy, meek and lowly, thou hast brought me to the valley of vision, where I live in the depths and see thee in the heights. Hemmed in by mountains of sin, I behold thy glory. Let me learn by paradox, the way down is the way up. To be low is to be high. To be brokenhearted is to be a healed heart. A contrite spirit is a rejoicing spirit. A repenting soul is the victorious soul.” And when I read that, it’s really a prayer of the beatitudinal wisdom. All these spiritual inversions. It gave me something to hold on to. And it also gave me a sense, which I remember thinking, that there is a moral order to the universe. I had a sense of this moral order before I had a sense of God, that this is so beautiful, these inversions. And there’s a structure to them, and it’s sort of an intellectual encompassing of everything that I love. I have a friend named David Wolpe who was a rabbi in L.A. He’s retired since. He had a passage which has rung in my mind, which I wanted to read to you to get your reaction. And he does not believe in “spiritual without religious.” And he writes this: “Spirituality is an emotion. Religion is an obligation. Spirituality soothes. Religion mobilizes. Spirituality is satisfied with itself. Religion is dissatisfied with the world.” Akhtar: I think my book is a direct contradiction of that orientation. I respect that quote a lot, and I think that it’s largely true, but it’s also clearly not. I’m interested by this idea that you’re at the top of the mountain and you’re having an experience, and in that moment you reach for language. I don’t. That’s the difference. And I don’t know what value that difference has for other people. I know that for me, reaching for language in that moment fixes the experience. And I want the experience to continue to exhibit that continuity that I was talking about earlier. That’s a technical matter, actually. By allowing it to be, it is allowed to have a different evolution. That’s just something that I’ve learned, that the meaning I could derive from the experience is ultimately less lasting and less valuable than continuing to relate to the experience. Brooks: But someone in your book says to the character, “You’re seeking states, not truth.” Now, when you’re talking about not reducing it to language, how do you retain it? Akhtar: The aspirant who hates God only has to be around for three more lifetimes. If you focus on it, you’re gonna retain something. Language is not a way to retain it. Language is a way to no longer relate to it. In my experience. So that’s why the challenge of the book was how to articulate this experience in a language. Between my last book and this book, I learned something about the sentence. Sentences for me before this book were about a meaning conveyed between punctuation. In this book, somehow the sentence became a way to move inquiry and energy across punctuation into the next sentence. And so it was like, in a way—like the scene with Bloom, what is the force that’s moving? There’s a movement that once it begins shouldn’t stop, and it should not be stopped by any meaning. It should not be stopped by any scene. There has to be some absorbing continuity that the reader is drawn into. Brooks: That gets me back to my friend Gregory of Nyssa. He’s about spiritual movement. I once read a book by a guy named John Coates, who’s a neuroscientist, who said, We didn’t evolve to solve problems. We evolved to move across a landscape . And he says, If you think of the brain as an organ designed to foster movement, you will never see yourself the same way again . And that’s true: Since I read that sentence, I’ve never seen it the same. Akhtar: And that’s what happened to me with the sentence, the writing of a sentence, understanding how a sentence could function with this book. That it functioned to move, not to fix. Brooks: Now, there’s a moment, and I keep ruining our conversation with neuroscience, but— Akhtar: There’s a lot of neuroscience in the book. Brooks: I know. That’s what I’m getting to. There’s a scene where the character’s like, What is going on in my brain that all this is happening? So he goes to a doctor. He says, Oh, your insula —which is a part of the brain— it’s growing . Akhtar: Thickened. Brooks: Now, should I see that scene as a de-sacralization of his experience, of his condition? I was somehow disappointed. He’s reducing it to the insula? And I’ve been guilty in the last conversation to do that, but— Akhtar: We all are. I think when the medical vocabulary enters our experience, it becomes the final vocabulary. It is our way of materializing that immaterial terror of death that we have. Because we’re so frightened of death, rightly so—or as Montaigne would say, not rightly so—that medical language, which is the primary language of mortality, and morality on some level in our culture becomes the final way to talk about anything. So it was impossible to write this book without including the medical map, without including the medical language. It’s been demonstrated that activation of this area of the insula that’s up against the temporal lobe creates religious experience. So what are the implications of that? What are the implications of there being a physiological corollary to the experience that the narrator’s having? Does it disqualify that experience? There’s lots of instances of the uncanny in the book as well. So that presumably is not explained by the brain scans, and yet all those things have to coexist because those are the languages of the 21st century. I didn’t wanna write a book that was not responsible to the languages that we live in. I wanted to write a book that at least attempted a process of restoring a magic—at least for me as a writer as I was writing it—of the inner life, because it felt to me that that was something that we’re all more and more sensitive to and longing for. David Brooks: C. S. Lewis, before he was—alongside of being the writer of the Narnia stories, he was a medievalist. He wrote about medieval literature. He said something was lost when humans used to look up to the night sky and they would see magic, enchanted. Now we see balls of gas burning that lie far away. Akhtar: That’s the opening quote of my book, by the way. György Lukács. There was a time when we would look up at the starry skies and see the map of all possibilities. Brooks: Have we lost something, or is there something we need to be on the watch out for as our culture has trended in this direction? Akhtar: I don’t know. I know that I don’t wanna lose it. And so my focus is not losing it. I focus as much as possible on that invisible, immaterial inner part of us that is the substance of our moral life. The Russians wrote about it beautifully. It’s why we still read the Russians. I don’t know why we got so timid writing about such things. So yeah, I think we certainly have lost something, but I don’t wanna lose it. Brooks: I do think that’s why I read the Russians too. That moment when, say, in Tolstoy, Prince Andrei is on the battlefield somewhere and he looks up at the endless vastness of the sky, or Levin is cutting grass and he has this experience of— Akhtar: Or Ivan Ilyich at the end is consumed and subsumed by a radiance. Brooks: And they’re not all happy people. They had the radiance, and they— Akhtar: I don’t think a fundamental orientation in soulfulness is about happiness. I think that the great saints and in all the traditions—and in your own tradition, Christ, he’s not happy. The lesson is not happiness. And I feel like that is part of the problem of our orientation to some of this stuff. Brooks: He could’ve been like, “Six life hacks to be a happy Messiah.” Akhtar: Happiness is overrated. Happiness of a certain ilk, I think, is overrated if you really wanna talk about this kind of stuff. Brooks: I would say some of the things that challenge my spiritual life are my achievement orientation, time orientation. There’s a lot you have to let go of, which I have trouble doing. You mentioned earlier—maybe we’ll close on this, because it’s a fascinating part of the novel and your own life that I can’t explain and don’t understand, which is you talked about your dreams and these coincidences that you often dream. Describe some of that and what it means to you. Akhtar: I still don’t understand it. I started keeping track of my dreams in college and then really accelerated that sort of focus on my nightlife, if you will, between the ages of 22 and 26 when I was sleeping with a pencil tied to my finger to remind me when I would get into that hypnagogic state that there was something I needed to write down. So I’d write down every dream. And during this period, one thing that started to happen with a degree of unpredictable regularity was that I would dream of something that seemed to then happen. I talk about it a little bit in The Atlantic essay, and it’s usually pretty prosaic stuff, but still didn’t make any sense why this would happen, and seemed to point to the fact that maybe space-time was not what we think it is. Even if I had no other way of knowing that. This has recurred throughout my life, as I’ve continued to pay attention to my dreams. Unfortunately, I’ve never seen any lottery numbers. So I don’t know what it means, but it clearly is a mystery and does point to there maybe being more in heaven and Earth than is contained in the kinds of books that I, and all of us, tend to read. That’s part of the novel as well. The psychoanalytic tradition does deal with this a bit because it’s a phenomenon that occurs relatively regularly within analytic settings at times. They have some sort of way of working with it, but it’s interesting. I don’t know what it means. I’m not sure what the utility of this strange proclivity that I’ve had, but I know that it’s a fact. It’s a subjective fact that I have to deal with. And it must tell me something about the world that I’m living in, which is different in essence than how it appears. Brooks: I hope people have listened to us and got a sense of how valuable and important this book is. I really mean that, because sometimes we’re feeling we’re fighting the shallowification of life. Maybe you would call it the rationalization, or Max Weber, the iron cage, or we’re now in a silicon cage. And to delve into these regions strikes me as the most important thing we can do to preserve our humanity. It’s not always easy, and it’s not always clear, but it’s where our efforts should be, and people should definitely buy this book. I don’t know if you have any closing thoughts. Ayad Akhtar: I’m just grateful, David. I’m so gratified to have this conversation with you, and I think the name of your new endeavor here, The Permanent Questions , is beautiful and right on. Brooks: One of the highlights for me of my conversation with Ayad is when he pushed back on the David Wolpe quote I read, criticizing people who are spiritual and not religious. He is spiritual and not religious, and I have to say he is more spiritually evolved certainly than me and maybe more than a lot of pastors I know. He has put in the work, done the reading from Plato to Meister Eckhart to Thomas Merton, and he’s constructed a spiritual sense. And it’s humbling to see that. The thing I 100 percent agree with him on is that we do our culture harm when we try to bleach spiritual talk out of our public conversation, public debate. Human beings, religious or not religious, are metaphysical creatures, and if you take that element out of our lives and out of our common lives, you’re doing real damage to your society and to the people in it. Thanks so much for joining us for this week’s conversation with Ayad Akhtar. The Permanent Questions is produced and edited by The Atlantic in partnership with Yale University. New episodes of The Permanent Questions come out on Sundays. You can subscribe on The Atlantic ’s YouTube channel, Apple, Spotify, or wherever you get your podcasts. If you wanna support this work and the work of my colleagues, you can subscribe to the publication at TheAtlantic.com/Listener. See you next week.

articles.title: Đề xuất sớm đưa hai cao tốc qua Lạng Sơn và Cao Bằng vào khai thác
articles.text:
Đề nghị giải phóng mặt bằng dứt điểm trong tháng 10
Cao tốc Đồng Đăng -Trà Lĩnh có tổng chiều dài tuyến 121,06km. Trong đó, giai đoạn 1 chiều dài 93,35km thực hiện quy mô cao tốc 4 làn xe hạn chế (mặt đường 17m).
Giai đoạn 2 sẽ mở rộng đoạn 1 và thi công mới phần còn lại theo quy mô 4 làn hoàn chỉnh, vận tốc thiết kế 80km/h. Tổng mức đầu tư dự án 26.184 tỷ đồng, trong đó vốn nhà đầu tư huy động 8.197 tỷ đồng; vốn Nhà nước 17.987 tỷ đồng.
Thời gian thực hiện giai đoạn 1: Khởi công năm 2024, hoàn thành đưa vào khai thác năm 2027. Giai đoạn 2: Khởi công năm 2025, hoàn thành năm 2028. Tuy nhiên theo chỉ đạo của Chính phủ, nhà đầu tư quyết tâm hoàn thành các dự án sớm hơn 1 năm so với kế hoạch.
Để đạt được mục tiêu trên, nhà đầu tư đề nghị UBND tỉnh Cao Bằng báo cáo Thủ tướng, bộ, ngành đảm bảo việc bổ sung 7.715 tỷ đồng vốn ngân sách nhà nước còn thiếu trong giai đoạn năm 2026 - 2028 theo quy định, tiến độ thi công.
Đề nghị UBND hai tỉnh Cao Bằng, Lạng Sơn và Bộ Xây dựng thống nhất báo cáo Chính phủ xem xét, cho phép tạm đưa đoạn tuyến Tân Thanh (Km0) - Đông Khê Km62) vào phục vụ miễn phí dịp Tết Nguyên đán 2027 trong điều kiện chưa hoàn thành nghiệm thu đồng bộ phần mở rộng giai đoạn 2.
UBND tỉnh Cao Bằng, Lạng Sơn chỉ đạo các cơ quan chức năng theo địa bàn (CSGT, Cảnh sát PCCC & CNCH, Y tế...) phối hợp với Cục Đường bộ Việt Nam, Tập đoàn Đèo Cả, doanh nghiệp dự án và đơn vị hỗ trợ vận hành HHV thống nhất phương án quản lý, vận hành.
Huy động nhân sự, phương tiện, thiết bị và tổ chức diễn tập các phương án PCCC & CHCN, điều tiết đảm bảo ATGT trên tuyến, đặc biệt tại các đoạn qua hầm.
Ông Hồ Minh Hoàng, Chủ tịch Tập đoàn Đèo Cả cho biết, đến nay, công tác GPMB phía Lạng Sơn còn một số vị trí xôi đỗ trên đường gom, đề nghị địa phương giải quyết dứt điểm trong tháng 10.
Hiện trạm dừng nghỉ đang GPMB, chưa thể hoàn thành trong năm 2026. Tuy nhiên nhà đầu tư đề nghị nghiệm thu có điều kiện, giúp phục vụ người dân lưu thông trong dịp Tết Nguyên đán.
Tranh thủ thời tiết, đẩy nhanh thi công
Báo cáo với Phó Thủ tướng Thường trực Chính phủ, Bộ trưởng Trần Hồng Minh cho biết: Đúng ra, dự án sẽ được hoàn thành trong năm 2027 và 2028 nhưng các địa phương và nhà đầu tư đã có nhiều cố gắng trong GPMB, khắc phục khó khăn, vướng mắc, gộp hai giai đoạn thực hiện đồng thời giúp dự án về đích trước 1 năm so với kế hoạch.
Bộ trưởng cũng cho rằng, tuy cuối năm nay, công tác thi công trạm dừng nghỉ chưa thể hoàn thành nhưng cần hoàn thiện các hạng mục còn lại, có phương án đưa cao tốc Hữu Nghị - Chi Lăng và đoạn từ Đồng Đăng, tỉnh Lạng Sơn đến Đông Khê, tỉnh Cao Bằng vào khai thác, phục vụ đi lại của người dân trong dịp Tết Nguyên đán năm 2027.
Lãnh đạo hai tỉnh Lạng Sơn và Cao Bằng cũng khẳng định sẽ giải quyết dứt điểm vướng mắc, hoàn thành GPMB các dự án trong tháng 10 tới.
Trực tiếp kiểm tra, chỉ đạo tại công trường, Phó Thủ tướng Thường trực Chính phủ Phạm Gia Túc chỉ đạo, hai tỉnh Lạng Sơn và Cao Bằng cần quyết liệt chỉ đạo, hoàn thành GPMB ngay trong tháng 10.
Các nhà thầu đang huy động tối đa máy móc đẩy nhanh tiến độ thi công các tuyến cao tốc qua Lạng Sơn và Cao Bằng.
Ngay khi có mặt bằng, nhà đầu tư cần tăng người, tăng máy, tranh thủ những ngày thời tiết đẹp đẩy nhanh tiến độ thi công; có giải pháp thi công an toàn, không để xảy ra sạt lở mái ta luy trong quá trình thi công, khai thác các dự án.
Đồng ý chủ trương nghiệm thu có điều kiện khi hoàn thành các dự án, Phó Thủ tướng Thường trực Chính phủ cho biết Chính phủ sẽ cùng các bộ, ngành đánh giá cụ thể trước khi triển khai. Tuy nhiên, để đủ điều kiện khai thác, các tuyến đường phải hoàn thiện cả 4 làn xe, có đầy đủ hệ thống ATGT theo tiêu chuẩn, quy chuẩn hiện hành.
Phó Thủ tướng cũng đề nghị tỉnh Lạng Sơn sớm hoàn thành xây dựng cửa khẩu thông minh để khai thác hiệu quả các tuyến đường.

articles.title: Anh: Sự cố nghiêm trọng gần căn cứ Không quân Mỹ dùng để tấn công Iran
articles.text:
TPO - Cảnh sát Anh ngày 27/9 đã bắt giữ một số người đàn ông vì nghi ngờ vi phạm các quy định về chất nổ gần RAF Fairford - căn cứ không quân được Mỹ sử dụng để tấn công các mục tiêu của Iran. Người dân ngôi làng gần đó đã phải sơ tán, trong khi cơ quan chức năng mô tả đây là một “sự cố nghiêm trọng”.
Chính phủ Anh - vốn đã cho phép Mỹ sử dụng căn cứ RAF Fairford để tấn công các mục tiêu Iran - cho biết Thủ tướng Andy Burnham đang được cập nhật thông tin về vụ việc.
Một nhân chứng của Reuters cho biết, cảnh sát vũ trang đã phong tỏa lối vào cổng chính của căn cứ, trong khi các loại máy móc hạng nặng được bố trí chắn trước các lối ra vào. Người dân tại một ngôi làng gần đó đã bị đánh thức vào sáng sớm và được yêu cầu rời khỏi nhà.
Khoảng 30 xe khẩn cấp, bao gồm xe cảnh sát, xe cứu thương và xe cứu hỏa, đã tập kết tại ngôi làng Fairford gần căn cứ, trong khi một chiếc trực thăng bay lượn phía trên.
"Một số khu vực dân cư đang được sơ tán sau khi sự việc được tuyên bố là một sự cố nghiêm trọng. Động thái này diễn ra sau vụ bắt giữ một số người đàn ông vì nghi ngờ vi phạm Đạo luật Chất nổ”, cảnh sát địa phương cho biết trong một tuyên bố. "Đội chuyên trách xử lý vật liệu nổ của quân đội hiện đang kiểm tra một số phương tiện”.
Cảnh sát cho biết tình hình hiện đã được kiểm soát.
Máy bay ném bom B-1B Lancer đỗ tại căn cứ không quân RAF Fairford - nơi có sự hiện diện của nhân sự Không quân Mỹ - ở Fairford (Anh) ngày 27/9. (Ảnh: Reuters)
Trang web của tờ Daily Mail đã đăng tải hình ảnh năm người đàn ông cởi trần đang bị bắt giữ, trong khi một bức ảnh khác cho thấy ba chiếc xe van lớn màu trắng đang đỗ gần đó.
Hình ảnh trực tiếp từ hiện trường do các đài truyền hình phát sóng cho thấy một robot xử lý bom đang hoạt động gần ba chiếc xe van này. Truyền thông địa phương đưa tin, cơ quan chống khủng bố đang chủ trì cuộc điều tra vụ việc.
Những người đàn ông bị bắt và ba chiếc xe van màu trắng. (Ảnh: Daily Mail)
Cảnh sát vũ trang tại hiện trường. (Ảnh: Reuters)
Chính phủ Anh cho biết sẽ không phù hợp để đưa ra bình luận khi cuộc điều tra vẫn đang diễn ra.
Một người phát ngôn của Không quân Mỹ từ chối thảo luận về các biện pháp bảo vệ lực lượng cụ thể.
Anh tuyên bố hồi tháng 7, rằng quân đội nước này đã sẵn sàng bảo vệ đất nước trước mọi cuộc tấn công, sau khi Lực lượng Vệ binh Cách mạng Hồi giáo Iran cảnh báo Anh không được cho phép máy bay ném bom của Mỹ cất cánh từ căn cứ Fairford.
Các phương tiện truyền thông đưa tin, an ninh đã được tăng cường tại những căn cứ khác mà Mỹ sử dụng ở Anh, bao gồm Lakenheath và Mildenhall.
TPO - Văn phòng Tổng thống Hàn Quốc đã yêu cầu Ukraine đưa ra lời giải thích chính thức và xin lỗi vì tiết lộ việc chuyển giao 2 tù binh Triều Tiên cho Seoul.
TPO - Theo các nhà phân tích, những căn cứ quân sự mà Washington đề xuất xây dựng, cùng với việc mở rộng hiện diện quân sự tại Greenland, sẽ giống như một tấm biển “tránh xa”, nhằm ngăn chặn khả năng Trung Quốc và Nga hợp tác quân sự tại Bắc cực.
TP - Trong bối cảnh nguy cơ cướp biển và những bất ổn trên một số tuyến hàng hải quốc tế đang trở thành vấn đề đáng quan tâm đối với hoạt động vận tải biển, Nga đang nhấn mạnh một lợi thế đặc biệt của Tuyến đường biển phương Bắc (NSR): các tàu đi qua vùng biển Bắc Cực không phải đối mặt mối đe dọa cướp biển, vận chuyển hàng hóa từ châu Á sang châu Âu chỉ mất khoảng một nửa thời gian so với hành trình đi qua kênh đào Suez, báo Nga News.ru đưa tin ngày 27/9.
TPO - Bộ Quốc phòng Nga tuyên bố lực lượng nước này đã tập kích một loạt mục tiêu hậu cần, thông tin liên lạc và cơ sở hạ tầng quân sự tại Ukraine, trong đó có trung tâm dữ liệu của Vodafone ở Kiev.
TPO - Các lực lượng vũ trang Iran sẵn sàng ứng phó với bất kỳ cuộc tấn công nào tái diễn từ phía Mỹ, theo người phát ngôn quân đội Mohammad Akraminia. Tuyên bố này được đưa ra sau khi Tổng thống Mỹ Donald Trump bác bỏ đề xuất của Iran về việc mở lại eo biển Hormuz và chấm dứt giao tranh.
TPO - Hai cá thể gấu trúc đã rời Thành Đô (Tây Nam Trung Quốc) vào sáng 27/9 để lên đường đến ngôi nhà mới tại Atlanta, theo một thỏa thuận giữa chính phủ Trung Quốc và Mỹ.
TPO - Hàng chục nghìn người vừa tập trung ở trung tâm thủ đô Madrid để phản đối cuộc khủng hoảng nhà ở tại Tây Ban Nha, yêu cầu tăng cường biện pháp bảo vệ người thuê nhà và cấm trục xuất người thuê nếu họ không có nơi ở nào khác.
TPO - Ngoại trưởng Đức Johann Wadephul và người đồng cấp Nga Sergey Lavrov vừa có cuộc gặp hiếm hoi bên lề kỳ họp Đại hội đồng Liên Hợp Quốc (LHQ). Đây là cuộc gặp trực tiếp đầu tiên giữa ngoại trưởng hai nước kể từ khi Nga mở chiến dịch quân sự đặc biệt tại Ukraine năm 2022.
TPO - Hàng trăm nghìn người chen kín đại lộ Champs-Élysées nổi tiếng của Paris để tham dự thánh lễ ngoài trời với Giáo hoàng Leo XIV, cho thấy sức hút lâu bền của Giáo hội Công giáo ở quốc gia từng rất sùng đạo nhưng hiện chính thức theo chế độ thế tục.
TPO - Trong bài phát biểu tại Đại hội đồng Liên Hợp Quốc ngày 26/9, Phó Chủ tịch nước Trung Quốc Hàn Chính nói rằng chủ quyền của các quốc gia ở khu vực Vịnh cần được tôn trọng, đồng thời kêu gọi “quốc gia liên quan” ngừng đe dọa và dỡ bỏ lệnh phong toả Cuba.

TPO - Giữa những bộ dao nĩa bằng bạc và những chiếc ly pha lê sáng bóng trên bàn quốc yến tại Nhà Trắng, người ta còn nhìn thấy hai chiếc bình giữ nhiệt mà Chủ tịch Trung Quốc Tập Cận Bình và Phu nhân Bành Lệ Viện mang theo.

Các chuyên gia nhìn nhận bước phát triển này trong bối cảnh hai nước đều đang tìm cách đa dạng hóa quan hệ kinh tế, củng cố khả năng chống chịu và duy trì quyền tự chủ trong môi trường quốc tế nhiều biến động.
TPO - Bốn tháng sau cuộc gặp gần nhất, Tổng thống Donald Trump và Chủ tịch Tập Cận Bình đã dành cho nhau những lời xã giao đẹp đẽ trong chuyến thăm đầu tiên của nhà lãnh đạo Trung Quốc tới Washington sau hơn một thập kỷ.

articles.title: The Kennedy Center Is the Most Terrifying Building in America
articles.text: Don’t you dare go inside the Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts! It’s much too dangerous. They have had murders there for 39 straight years —every night, and some matinees too. And they still haven’t caught the culprit. Nightly murders, with groups of middle schoolers sitting there, applauding. Murders in a hair salon, of all places! Sheer madness. It is not just the murder capital of Washington. Revolutions happen there, frequently. They built a barricade on one of the stages and tried to take down the whole French government. And they sang the whole time. This is the kind of thing that the Kennedy Center harbors and abets. They shot Alexander Hamilton there, not just once, but nightly, to make sure he was really dead. People went Into the Woods and got trampled by a giant. A rat king danced there. Valkyries rode there. Fairies forced people to fall in love, then out of love. It all happened in this building. The falling ceiling is the least of anyone’s concerns. Everything else about this place is far more threatening. And it’s not just murders and revolutions and dancing rodents. Horrifying transformations happened. They tested out new technologies there, called “plays.” (They even tested a couple of mine .) People got handed sheets of paper to read from and stood behind music stands and became other people . A very dangerous device, the play, and the Kennedy Center encouraged it. The most diabolical thing was that you did not always need to pay for these things. They just gave them away, free, every afternoon, for decades, to anyone who wanted to come in and watch. They gave them away online too! And nobody prevented this! This place encouraged other, equally frightening things. Dance, music. These performers didn’t even speak with words, just moved their bodies around and blew wind through metal tubes and reeds and scratched at strings—and people left the room in tears. What was the music saying? What were the bodies saying? The audience seemed to understand, but there were no words to help them. If people can communicate like this, then how can speech be properly controlled? If people can understand one another just by scratching a bow across taut strings—perhaps this is a form of witchcraft. No place that tolerates it must be permitted to stand. A blue figure stood guard outside. Dancing? Kicking? There was ambiguity, and that was scary. Sometimes people recorded podcasts there. Sometimes they watched movies on the lawn outside. Sometimes they played the tuba. They gathered together and experienced things together, and that, we can agree, was dangerous. There was comedy and drama and voices you only dreamed of hearing in person. There were discussions and readings. People learned things of which they had been previously unaware. There were chimes and fountains and overpriced intermission snacks. They dared to invite children into this place too. They dared to sit them down and tell them stories, on a stage. Do you know what a story can do to a mind? Do you know how long that story can linger before exploding into life, decades later? The Kennedy Center is the deadliest condemned building in America. For 55 years, people have been going in and coming out changed . Not physically, not visibly, but inside, carrying dangerous stories with them. Carrying music that could sustain them through times of trial, or the encouragement of shared laughter, or the seditious sense that they were not alone. Root it out! Stamp it out! Knock it down with a wrecking ball! This building is much too dangerous.

articles.title: Đồng Nai: Yêu cầu hoàn trả nguyên trạng lòng sông Buông trước 30/9
articles.text:
Ngày 27/9, UBND TP Đồng Nai có văn bản yêu cầu các sở, ngành và địa phương khẩn trương triển khai giải pháp xử lý tình trạng ngập úng tại khu vực sông Buông, phường Phước Tân, trong đó chú ý bảo đảm dòng chảy và khả năng tiêu thoát nước.
Theo đó, Chủ tịch UBND TP Đồng Nai giao Ban QLDA đầu tư xây dựng công trình giao thông TP Đồng Nai chỉ đạo nhà thầu khẩn trương tháo dỡ các công trình tạm, cầu tạm, cống tạm phục vụ thi công dự án thành phần 1 cao tốc Biên Hòa - Vũng Tàu. Việc tháo dỡ phải bảo đảm không ảnh hưởng dòng chảy và hoàn trả nguyên trạng lòng sông Buông trước ngày 30/9.
Ban QLDA cũng được yêu cầu rà soát, đánh giá toàn bộ hệ thống thoát nước ngang, thoát nước dọc của dự án, bảo đảm công trình không ảnh hưởng đến khả năng thoát nước tự nhiên tại khu vực. Kết quả phải báo cáo Sở Xây dựng TP Đồng Nai trước ngày 30/9.
Về lâu dài, UBND TP Đồng Nai giao Sở Nông nghiệp và Môi trường chủ trì, phối hợp Sở Xây dựng và các đơn vị liên quan nghiên cứu phương án thoát nước toàn lưu vực sông Buông, đề xuất giải pháp xử lý dứt điểm tình trạng ngập tại phường Phước Tân. Kết quả báo cáo UBND TP trước ngày 15/10.
UBND phường Phước Tân được giao kiểm tra, xử lý các trường hợp xây dựng lấn chiếm làm ảnh hưởng dòng chảy tự nhiên của sông Buông, đồng thời thanh thải chướng ngại vật cản trở tiêu thoát nước.
Khu dân cư gần cao tốc Biên Hoà - Vũng Tàu liên tục bị ngập, ảnh hưởng đến đời sống người dân.
Trước đó, khu dân cư Hương Phước, phường Phước Tân liên tục xảy ra ngập, ảnh hưởng đến đời sống người dân. Ngày 15/9, Ban QLDA phối hợp các đơn vị liên quan kiểm tra khu vực cống ngang tại Km 1+950 và cầu sông Buông tại Km 2+574, sau khi Sở Nông nghiệp và Môi trường báo cáo về nguyên nhân ngập tại khu dân cư ven sông.
Theo báo cáo, địa phương cho rằng cống thoát nước qua cao tốc Biên Hòa - Vũng Tàu tại Km 1+950 bị đặt lệch so với dòng chảy hiện hữu, gây khó khăn cho việc tiêu thoát nước về hạ lưu.
Qua rà soát hồ sơ và kiểm tra hiện trường, Ban QLDA bước đầu xác định cống ngang và cầu vượt sông Buông được thiết kế, thi công theo hồ sơ đã được phê duyệt. Đơn vị cũng cho biết tình trạng ngập tại khu phố Hương Phước đã xảy ra nhiều năm, trước khi dự án cao tốc được triển khai.
Cụ thể, năm 2008, khu dân cư từng ngập sâu 1,5-2m; các năm 2016, 2019 và 2022 tiếp tục xảy ra ngập. Riêng tháng 10/2024, nhiều khu vực ngập sâu 1-1,7m, thời gian ngập kéo dài đến 48 giờ.
Theo nhận định của Ban QLDA, tình trạng bồi lắng khiến lòng sông Buông ngày càng nông, dòng chảy bị thu hẹp là một trong những nguyên nhân dẫn đến ngập. Khu dân cư Hương Phước nằm ở vùng trũng thấp, cuối nguồn sông Buông nên khả năng tiêu thoát nước cũng hạn chế khi lưu lượng từ thượng nguồn tăng cao.
Ngoài việc tháo dỡ cầu tạm và hoàn trả lòng sông, Ban QLDA sẽ đo đạc, đánh giá khả năng thoát nước của cống tại Km 1+950 để đề xuất phương án xử lý.
Về lâu dài, đơn vị đề xuất cải tạo, mở rộng khoảng 6,9km sông Buông và 2,9km rạch Bà Bướm, với tổng mức đầu tư dự kiến hơn 4.300 tỷ đồng.

articles.title: Học sinh lớp 9 tử vong khi tham gia trải nghiệm
articles.text:
TPO - Một học sinh lớp 9 Trường Tiểu học, THCS & THPT Albert Einstein (Hà Tĩnh) tử vong trong thời gian tham gia chương trình trải nghiệm tại TP Huế. Hiện cơ quan chức năng đang điều tra, làm rõ nguyên nhân.
Ngày 27/9, thông tin từ Sở GD&ĐT Hà Tĩnh, đơn vị vừa nhận được báo cáo từ Trường Tiểu học, THCS & THPT Albert Einstein liên quan đến sự việc học sinh lớp 9 của một trường tử vong khi tham gia trải nghiệm tại Huế.
Theo báo cáo của trường, từ tối 25/9 đến ngày 27/9, Trường Tiểu học, THCS & THPT Albert Einstein (đóng tại phường Thành Sen, tỉnh Hà Tĩnh) tổ chức chương trình trải nghiệm tại TP Huế cho 178 học sinh khối 9.
Ngôi trường nơi tổ chức cho học sinh tham gia trải nghiệm.
Khoảng 3h ngày 27/9, trong thời gian đoàn lưu trú tại một khách sạn trên đường Trần Cao Vân, phường Thuận Hóa, TP Huế, em N.M.Q. (SN 2012, học sinh lớp 9A5) được phát hiện tử vong sau khi rơi từ tầng 5 của khách sạn.
Hiện nguyên nhân vụ việc đang được cơ quan chức năng điều tra, làm rõ.
TPO - Hôm nay và ngày mai (28-29/9), miền Bắc tiếp tục oi nóng với nhiệt độ cao nhất dự báo 35-36 độ. Từ đêm 30/9, miền Bắc đón không khí lạnh yếu. Sau nhiều ngày mưa dông, hôm nay hầu hết khu vực miền Trung, Tây Nguyên ít mưa, riêng Nam Bộ mưa rải rác vào chiều và tối.
TPO - Tuần qua (từ 21 đến 27/9), Thủ tướng Chính phủ có các quyết định điều động, bổ nhiệm Thứ trưởng Bộ Xây dựng, Thứ trưởng Bộ Công thương, Phó Chủ nhiệm Văn phòng Chính phủ; phê chuẩn kết quả bầu chức vụ Chủ tịch UBND tỉnh Thái Nguyên và Chủ tịch UBND tỉnh Quảng Trị.
TP - Xuất phát từ ý tưởng giữ cá lại với dòng sông, người dân vùng đầu nguồn Hồng Ngự (Đồng Tháp) đã biến đoạn bờ kè bình dị thành “bến đỗ an toàn” của đàn cá hàng nghìn con. Cá được cho ăn, bảo vệ và sinh trưởng tự nhiên. Mô hình độc đáo này không chỉ góp phần bảo vệ nguồn lợi thủy sản mà còn đánh thức tình yêu thiên nhiên trong cộng đồng.
TPO - Tổng Bí thư, Chủ tịch nước Tô Lâm cho rằng “một việc nhỏ như thiếu sách giáo khoa thôi, mặc dù đã được tập trung giải quyết, nhưng cũng để lại những bài học trong trách nhiệm tổ chức thực hiện của các cơ quan chức năng”. Về bữa ăn học đường, Hà Nội có thể đầu tư một số trung tâm sản xuất suất ăn theo kinh nghiệm của các nước.
TPO - Sau những trận mưa lớn liên tục, nhiều vị trí mái taluy tại dự án thành phần 1 cao tốc Biên Hòa - Vũng Tàu, đoạn qua phường Phước Tân, TP Đồng Nai, xuất hiện tình trạng xói lở, sạt trượt, một số rãnh thoát nước bằng bê tông bị gãy, nền đất phía dưới bị khoét sâu.
TPO - Tổng Bí thư, Chủ tịch nước Tô Lâm thông tin, theo báo cáo của UBND TP. Hà Nội, có 92% người dân đồng tình với quy hoạch Hồ Gươm. “Như thế này mà không nhanh được nữa thì phụ lòng tin của người dân”, Tổng Bí thư, Chủ tịch nước nói.
