articles.title: ‘Cá mập’ Phố Wall đồng loạt tăng gom tiền mặt, điều gì đang xảy ra?
articles.text:
Theo khảo sát mới nhất của Marsh, một trong những công ty tư vấn đầu tư uy tín hàng đầu thế giới, dòng tiền vào tiền mặt đang tăng với tốc độ nhanh nhất từng được ghi nhận. Báo cáo được thực hiện với 430 tổ chức quản lý tài sản toàn cầu, đại diện cho tổng quy mô danh mục lên tới 5.760 tỷ USD.
Câu hỏi đặt ra là: Điều gì đang khiến những nhà đầu tư chuyên nghiệp, hiểu rõ thị trường nhất, lại đồng loạt rút lui và nắm giữ tiền mặt?
Tiền mặt trở thành điểm tựa phòng thủ
37,8% số tổ chức được hỏi cho biết họ dự định tăng tỷ trọng tiền mặt trong 12 tháng tới, tăng mạnh so với mức 9% của khảo sát năm trước. Đây là mức tăng mạnh nhất trong tất cả các nhóm tài sản được khảo sát, một sự thay đổi chóng mặt chỉ trong vòng một năm.
Đáng chú ý hơn, ý định phân bổ ròng vào tiền mặt đã tăng thêm 35,5 điểm phần trăm, đưa mức này lên dương 22%.
Nói một cách dễ hiểu, số nhà đầu tư muốn tăng nắm giữ tiền mặt hiện nhiều hơn hẳn số người muốn giảm. Đây là một tín hiệu rõ ràng cho thấy giới đầu tư chuyên nghiệp đang ưu tiên thanh khoản và sự an toàn lên hàng đầu.
Ngược lại, cổ phiếu Mỹ và cổ phiếu Anh lại là hai nhóm tài sản duy nhất ghi nhận xu hướng bị giảm tỷ trọng.
Tỷ lệ phân bổ ròng đối với cổ phiếu Mỹ đã giảm xuống mức -10,3%, trong khi cổ phiếu Anh thậm chí còn tệ hơn với mức -16,5%. Điều này có nghĩa là có nhiều nhà đầu tư muốn bán ra hơn là mua vào hai thị trường chứng khoán lớn này.
Vì sao các nhà đầu tư lớn tăng nắm giữ tiền mặt?
Câu trả lời nằm ở 2 từ: địa chính trị và lạm phát. Khảo sát được thực hiện trong tháng 6 và tháng 7 cho thấy rủi ro địa chính trị và lạm phát là hai yếu tố được quan tâm nhiều nhất, khi hơn 70% số tổ chức tham gia đánh giá đây là những yếu tố có ảnh hưởng lớn tới quyết định đầu tư trong ngắn hạn.
Ông Amit Popat, Giám đốc toàn cầu mảng định chế tài chính của Marsh, nhận định rằng hơn 3/4 số nhà đầu tư được hỏi đã gọi rủi ro địa kinh tế là mối đe dọa hàng đầu.
Việc tăng tỷ trọng tiền mặt, theo ông, là để "cung cấp thành phần phòng thủ trong một môi trường không chắc chắn", đồng thời tạo ra sự linh hoạt cần thiết để nắm bắt những cơ hội bất ngờ xuất hiện.
Nói cách khác, các nhà đầu tư đang chủ động xây dựng một vị thế mới. Ông Niall O'Sullivan, Giám đốc đầu tư toàn cầu của Marsh, đã mô tả chiến lược này bằng một thuật ngữ đáng chú ý: "barbell".
Theo ông, các nhà quản lý tài sản đang "tăng cường các tài sản mang tính phòng thủ để giảm rủi ro, vừa duy trì sự linh hoạt nhằm sẵn sàng nắm bắt cơ hội nếu thị trường biến động".
Theo cách tiếp cận này, tiền mặt vừa đóng vai trò phòng thủ, vừa tạo dư địa để nhà đầu tư nhanh chóng phân bổ vốn khi xuất hiện cơ hội.
Không chỉ có tiền mặt: Dòng tiền đang chảy về đâu?
Nếu chỉ nhìn vào con số tiền mặt, người ta có thể nghĩ rằng các nhà đầu tư đang rút lui hoàn toàn khỏi thị trường. Nhưng thực tế phức tạp hơn thế. Họ đang dịch chuyển dòng tiền sang những khu vực được cho là ít rủi ro hơn hoặc có tiềm năng sinh lời dài hạn tốt hơn.
Hơn một nửa số tổ chức được khảo sát (51%) dự định tăng tỷ trọng đầu tư vào hạ tầng trong 12 tháng tới. Đây được xem là một lĩnh vực đầu tư dài hạn, cung cấp thu nhập ổn định và ít bị ảnh hưởng bởi những biến động ngắn hạn của thị trường.
Gần một nửa số nhà đầu tư (47%) muốn gia tăng tiếp xúc với cổ phiếu tại các thị trường mới nổi và 41% hướng đến các tài sản liên kết lạm phát như một hàng rào bảo vệ trước sự xói mòn sức mua của đồng tiền.
Một điểm đáng chú ý là xu hướng giảm phụ thuộc vào một thị trường đơn lẻ đang trở nên đặc biệt rõ nét tại khu vực châu Á - Thái Bình Dương. Có tới 53% nhà đầu tư trong khu vực đã điều chỉnh phân bổ địa lý của mình trong vòng 1 năm qua, cao hơn mức gần 50% của bình quân toàn cầu.
Điều này cho thấy các nhà đầu tư châu Á đang nhạy bén hơn trong việc đa dạng hóa danh mục để giảm thiểu rủi ro tập trung.
Theo SCMP, The Business Times, Marsh, Business Wire, CNBC Africa

articles.title: Make It Loud With These Tested Party Speakers
articles.text:
The best party speakers are introducing the idea of raving anywhere to a whole new generation who may have missed the classic block-party boom box of the 1980s. These new speakers look like compact PA systems, and often sound just as loud, with bold and brash looks and bass-heavy profiles. They’re honestly a huge amount of fun.
The rising popularity of party speakers coincides with a broader shift toward entertaining at home rather than in bars and nightclubs, particularly among younger consumers. A July 2026 Harris Poll found that 68 percent of US Gen Z adults say going out is just too expensive, while Attest found that 64 percent now drink primarily at home, up from 42 percent a year earlier.
Where people socialize may be changing, but the need for good atmosphere certainly isn’t. Traditional Bluetooth speakers are convenient and sound great, but they struggle to bring the party. Party speakers, with their serious volume, portability, and LED lights, don’t have that problem.
For more audio guidance, check out WIRED's guides to the Best Bluetooth Speakers, Best Turntables, and Best Computer Speakers.
What Is a Party Speaker?
Party speakers are large, high-output Bluetooth speakers designed for social gatherings, sitting somewhere between a conventional wireless speaker and a portable PA. Current battery-powered models range from around 100 to 800 watts of power, with most offering between 12 to 25 hours of battery life, if not more. Expect large drivers, bass-boost modes, LED lighting, handles, wheels, and even replaceable batteries to keep the party going. Microphone and instrument inputs, karaoke controls, and the ability to link multiple speakers are also common, as are partner apps that give you the chance to play DJ, curate the lighting, and alter the sound.
How I Test Party Speakers
I’ve tested party speakers indoors and out, and at background, party, and ear-bleeding volumes. Sound quality is still important, but it’s party time, so bass, vocal clarity, and minimal distortion are key, as is how well the sound can travel (especially outdoors). Karaoke testing was dutifully undertaken by a gaggle of excitable but discerning tweenagers.
As well as playing rave classics at top volume (sorry, neighbors), I’ve analyzed the various EQ and control apps, AI features, digital signal processing (DSP) modes, and the speaker's ability to pair with DJ equipment, separate sources, and musical instruments.
What Should I Look for in a Party Speaker?
Power: Party speakers range from boxes one person can comfortably carry to 60-pound-plus towers on wheels. Power varies, but I’ve tested designs from 100 to 800-plus watts. As a general rule, the more watts it can output, the louder it will be, but clever DSP means brands like JBL and Sony can often make more noise with less watts than you might think.
Battery life: Your needs will again depend on how you party, but between 12 to 25 hours is common. Remember, though, high volume and lighting can cut that number down. Soundboks, for example, quotes 40 hours at mid volume but only six to eight hours at maximum, depending on the speaker.
Connectivity: As well as Bluetooth for wireless convenience, 3.5-mm or other line inputs are useful for DJ controllers, mixers, and sources beyond your phone, while some models add RCA, quarter-inch, or XLR connections. Outdoor users should look for an IP rating. Replaceable batteries, wheels, sturdy handles, and physical controls become considerably more important once a speaker leaves the living room.
Can I Use a Party Speaker With DJ Decks?
Yes, provided it has a suitable wired input. DJ controllers and mixers typically have a line-out option, commonly through RCA, quarter-inch, or XLR connections, although a 3.5-mm aux input can also work with the right cable.
If you are mixing, use a cable where possible, as Bluetooth introduces enough latency between moving a control and hearing the result to make accurate cueing and beat-matching difficult. Some specialist DJ systems like the Aiaiai Unit-4 Wireless+ Studio Monitors use proprietary low-latency wireless connections to get around this, but ordinary Bluetooth isn’t designed for the job.
What About Karaoke?
There’s plenty of crossover between party speakers and karaoke machines, but they’re not always the same thing. Some party speakers include one or two microphone inputs, while better-equipped models add wireless mics, separate vocal volume, echo or reverb, ample controls, and even vocal removal. The $350 Soundcore Rave 3S, for example, includes two wireless microphones and real-time vocal removal.
A dedicated karaoke setup puts singing rather than music playback first, and may offer more extensive microphone controls, song management, and accessories. WIRED’s Best Karaoke Gear guide covers those options in more detail.
How Do I Connect Multiple Phones to the Same Bluetooth Speaker?
Bluetooth multipoint lets two phones stay connected simultaneously, although switching between them varies by speaker. For larger groups, Spotify Jam and Apple Music SharePlay let guests choose music from their own phones while one device stays connected to the speaker. YouTube Music also supports collaborative playlists, enabling several people to add songs in advance or during the party.
Best Overall Party Speaker
LG xboom Stage 501 Specs
| Battery Life | Up to 25 hours | 
| Dust/Water Resistance | IPX4 | 
| Connectivity | Bluetooth 6.1 with multipoint, Auracast, USB-C audio, USB-A, 3.5-mm aux input, two 6.3-mm mic inputs | 
| Special Features | AI karaoke, AI lighting, app EQ and DJ effects, replaceable battery | 
| Dimensions | 11.7 x 23.4 x 11.6 inches | 
| Weight | 25.8 pounds | 
The Stage 501 turned the open workshop next to my testing studio into something close to a daytime rave (minus the crowd and superstar DJ). Bass was deep and clean, and carried easily across the room. Even when it was so loud I couldn’t hear myself think, there was volume to spare. And best of all, it sounded good, not just loud.
Part of LG’s xboom collaboration with producer, Black Eyed Peas star, and tech obsessive will.i.am, it has twin 5.25-inch woofers and two 2.5-inch full-range drivers. There’s 160 watts available on battery and 220 watts when plugged in. The battery is replaceable and lasts up to 25 hours. At full power, with the light show on, it’s less than that, but still more than enough for me.
There are louder and larger options here, but for me, the Stage 501 strikes the ideal balance between outright party power and decent sound quality. It even manages to impress at normal indoor listening volumes, which is often the downfall of party speakers.
LG has embraced the sillier side of the genre too. The app gives you EQ, AI karaoke, synchronized lighting, and DJ effects that are a bit cringe but hard to ignore. Two built-in phone/tablet stands are genuinely useful for karaoke, and there are twin mic inputs, though microphones are sold separately.
At 25.8 pounds, the cabinet remains manageable enough for me to move around on my own, but it is still a big unit to carry and find space for. If it’s too big, the smaller xboom Stage 301 keeps much of the same styling and app functionality, just in a much smaller package.
My Favorite Party Speaker
JBL PartyBox 130 Specs
| Battery Life | Up to 15 hours | 
| Dust/Water Resistance | IPX4 | 
| Connectivity | Bluetooth 6.0, Auracast, USB-C, 3.5-mm aux, optical, mic/guitar inputs | 
| Special Features | AI Sound Boost, Smart EQ, light show, app control, replaceable battery | 
| Dimensions | 11.7 x 22.6 x 11.9 inches | 
| Weight | 24.8 pounds | 
At 24.8 pounds, the JBL PartyBox 130 isn’t exactly lightweight, but its modest size hits the sweet spot for me in my city home and garden. It’s solidly built, has impressive power for the size, and can be moved without risking my fragile L5 vertebrae.
Two 5.25-inch woofers and a pair of 1-inch tweeters produce 200 watts of output, with plenty of bass and enough volume to get a decent-sized party moving. JBL’s AI Sound Boost uses DSP (clever digital wizardry) to keep distortion under control as the volume rises, while an automatic EQ adjusts the balance depending on what’s playing. Both work well, although I got better results tweaking the EQ myself in the app, and for my ears, the LG xboom Stage 501 still outperforms this speaker.
The light show on this speaker is one of the best, and the app has a collection of lighting and DJ effects that range from fun to downright silly. Big, easy-to-use physical controls on the top of the speaker also make it easy to use without reaching for my phone.
The 15-hour replaceable battery feels a little short, but a 10-minute charge gives another 80 minutes of raving. The speaker is IPX4 splash-proof and has Auracast, optical, USB-C, and aux connections, plus dual mic and guitar inputs.
Best Premium Party Speaker
Marshall Bromley 450 Specs
| Battery Life | 40+ hours | 
| Dust/Water Resistance | IP55 | 
| Connectivity | Bluetooth 5.3 with multipoint, Auracast, RCA, USB-C, 3.5-mm in/out, two XLR/6.35-mm combo inputs | 
| Special Features | 360-degree stereo, reactive lighting, mic/instrument inputs, replaceable battery | 
| Dimensions | 14.4 x 10.3 x 19.4 inches | 
| Weight | 27.2 pounds | 
Marshall has been bringing the party with its speakers since 1962, so its recent foray into Bluetooth party speakers isn’t much of a stretch. The brand's first release was the $1,300 Bromley 750, an enormous, hugely impressive party speaker that makes you look like a roadie.
But for most people and typical house parties, the smaller but still premium Bromley 450 is a much more manageable option. At 27.2 pounds, it’s still hefty, but it packs the punch of a small PA system.
It also looks the part, with Marshall’s signature black-and-brass finish and metal grille giving proper rock-and-roll vibes. Maybe I’m just old, but the classic design feels more authentic than the modern LED-loaded Bluetooth boxes. (The tiny reactive LEDs, however, feel a little limp compared to its rivals.)
Two 6.5-inch woofers powered by 90-watt Class D amps, plus four full-range drivers with 55 watts each and a pair of passive radiators (400 watts total power) provide plenty of volume. The 360-degree arrangement spreads sound impressively around a large room or garden, and bass is powerful without overpowering everything else. If you prefer your vocals front and center-, you may want to spend some time tweaking the EQ in the app regardless.
Connectivity is anything but retro, with Auracast, multipoint, RCA, USB-C, aux, and twin mic/instrument inputs. The physical controls are particularly nice and a joy to use. The replaceable battery lasts an impressive 40-plus hours, while IP55 protection makes this speaker genuinely usable outdoors without having to baby it.
Best Value Party Speaker
Soundcore Rave 3S Specs
| Battery Life | Up to 12 hours | 
| Dust/Water Resistance | IPX4 | 
| Connectivity | Bluetooth 5.3 with multipoint, Auracast, TWS, 3.5-mm aux, 6.35-mm mic/guitar input | 
| Special Features | Two wireless microphones, AI Vocal Removal, four reverb modes, customizable lighting, app EQ, BassUp | 
| Dimensions | 21.7 x 12.0 x 11.1 inches | 
| Weight | 23.1 pounds | 
With two wireless microphones and ingenious AI Vocal Removal that extracts the vocal track from almost any song you stream, the Rave 3S is already WIRED’s favorite karaoke speaker. But its 200-watt output, strong bass, and impressive beat-synced lighting also make it a solid party speaker.
The AI vocal removal tool is impressive, and much better than the party trick I thought it might be. It isn’t flawless— it occasionally leaves traces of vocals in a song, but it’s customizable via the Soundcore app, and more than capable of enabling enthusiastic duets with Olivia Rodrigo.
A 6.5-inch woofer and three 2.5-inch full-range drivers are loud and clear without sounding too bass-heavy, although if you’re looking for more boom with your bap, there is a BassUp mode that pushes the lower frequencies hard.
At 23.1 pounds, with a well-balanced handle, it’s fairly easy to move about, although being the size and weight of a full carry-on bag, it would benefit from wheels. My only other gripe is that the quoted 12-hour battery life doesn’t compete with the best, and it fell short of that figure in testing.
Best Party Speaker for Deejaying
Sony ULT Tower 7 Specs
| Battery Life | Up to 30 hours | 
| Dust/Water Resistance | IPX4 | 
| Connectivity | Bluetooth 5.3 with multipoint, RCA in, XLR in/out, USB-A, USB-C, 6.3-mm mic input | 
| Special Features | 360-degree Party Sound, 2x bass modes, 10-band EQ, party lighting, Party Chain, DJ input, replaceable battery | 
| Dimensions | 16.6 x 28.0 x 13.7 inches | 
| Weight | 50.3 pounds | 
Sony’s new ULT range of speakers stretches from the relatively manageable $450 ULT Tower 5 to the frankly ridiculous $1,200 ULT Tower Max. Sitting between them is the ULT Tower 7, with excellent sound, an ample selection of inputs, a combined 420 watts of output, and a 30-hour battery. Be warned, though, while it’s smaller than the Tower Max, it is still absolutely enormous and weighs 50.3 pounds.
Most party speakers will accept music from a DJ controller, but Sony goes further with RCA and balanced XLR inputs, plus an XLR output for expanding a wired setup. Auracast-based Party Chain can also connect up to 100 compatible speakers, so you can go head-to-head with Madison Square Garden on volume.
Inside is an 11-inch woofer, two 4.7-inch midrange drivers, and four tweeters, including a rear-facing pair that spread audio around the room. Bass is deep and effective, and at close quarters with the volume cranked, I could really feel it. It’s not quite bone-shaking at the club levels, but it’s still impressive.
The 360-degree driver configuration helps sound spread out and avoid sounding too boxed in, and while the bass is still quite directional, I really enjoyed the scale and ease with which this speaker filled the room.
If you have the budget and space, and you want to play loud all night, the Sony delivers, but I do wish it had a retractable handle. The built-in corner handles are OK-, but you need to angle it sharply at an odd angle to engage the wheels, and trust me, you don’t want to carry this speaker by hand very far.
Best Compact Party Speaker
Sony ULT Field 7 Specs
| Battery Life | Up to 30 hours | 
| Dust/Water Resistance | IP67 | 
| Connectivity | Bluetooth 5.2 with multipoint, 3.5-mm aux, USB-A, 6.3-mm mic/guitar input | 
| Special Features | 2x bass modes, 7-band EQ, LDAC, Party Connect, Stereo Pair, ambient lighting, karaoke/guitar mode, USB phone charging | 
| Dimensions | 20.2 x 8.8 x 8.7 inches | 
| Weight | 13.9 pounds | 
After testing the ULT Tower 7, JBL, and LG xboom models, Sony’s Field 7 felt positively pocket-sized. It sits at the junction between full party speaker and oversize Bluetooth speaker, and makes a great case for both. I think it’s ideal as a hi-fi replacement in a college dorm or apartment that can also escape outside.
The 13.9-pound cylindrical design is certainly different, but it’s well made, and can be used vertically or horizontally (though the vertical orientation does scream ashtray to me).
Sound is satisfyingly big for something you can easily pick up and carry. There’s plenty of depth and weight to the bass, and it kept a houseful of girls dancing in the garden without getting distorted. Just as importantly, at lower volumes, it remains controlled enough to work as an everyday speaker rather than something you only wheel out for parties.
The illuminated end rings are fun once the sun goes down, although plenty of rivals do the same trick better. More useful is the IP67 rating and excellent 30-hour battery life, which means this speaker really will survive soggy, grubby, festival style conditions.
There are also mic/guitar and aux inputs, and two levels of bass to choose from, plus a good smattering of inputs, as well as multipoint Bluetooth. It’s not designed to rattle windows, but it is a more practical size and weight without massively compromising on party volume.
Best Rugged Party Speaker
Soundboks Rider Specs
| Battery Life | Up to 35 hours at mid volume; 8 hours at full volume; swappable battery pack | 
| Dust/Water Resistance | IP66 | 
| Connectivity | Bluetooth 4.2, 3.5-mm aux | 
| Special Features | 118-dB max output, Adaptive Bass Enhancer DSP, app EQ and sound profiles, removable steel grille | 
| Dimensions | 13.8 x 9.4 x 7.9 inches | 
| Weight | 14.3 pounds | 
WIRED editor Harry Rabinowitz tested the small but mighty Soundboks Rider and found a punchy, portable party speaker that swaps flashing lights and karaoke for serious volume and durability.
At 14.3 pounds it is much easier to move than most party speakers, but an 8-inch woofer and 1.2-inch tweeter still generate up to 118 dB of sound. Harry described the output as “astonishing,” especially as it stayed clear and detailed across the volume range, with bass that didn't overwhelm.
It’s also built for considerably rougher treatment than the average speaker, with a steel grille, thick plastic cabinet, and silicone ball corners. During his drop test, Rabinowitz was more worried about damaging his stairs than the speaker. IP66 dust and water resistance makes it well suited to outdoor use too.
The swappable battery lasts up to 35 hours at mid volume, or eight hours at full blast, which is up there with the best. It also charges over USB-C, which is very convenient for most people.
It's not without compromise, however. Especially given the price, Bluetooth 4.2 feels very old, and connectivity is limited to a 3.5-mm aux input. For $600, it is niche, but if your priorities are portability, durability, and huge, clean sound over party gimmicks, the Rider is difficult to ignore.

articles.title: OLPC XO-1: The price of free
articles.text:
The idea was big, exciting, and inspiring: What if we could get every kid in the world access to a computer? For a bunch of thinkers and executives in Silicon Valley, it felt like the way to fix everything. But the One Laptop Per Child initiative, and the XO-1 laptop designed to be given away, were both more complicated than anyone expected.
Why OLPC’s $100 laptop never stood a chance
On Version History: David Imel and Adi Robertson debate if the OLPC XO-1 was innovative hardware or just a bad idea.
In the next episode of Version History, David Pierce is joined by The Verge’s Adi Robertson and tech journalist David Imel to figure out why OLPC didn’t work, whether there’s anything to learn from the XO-1’s innovative design, and if this kind of computer giveaway could ever succeed.
We’re halfway through the fifth season of Version History and we’ve been touring the educational tech icons in schools. If you missed hearing from the lead game designer of Oregon Trail or just how much The Verge’s Nilay Patel loved his TI-82 graphing calculator, check out those episodes here: :

articles.title: Giá vàng hôm nay 27/9/2026 lao dốc, vàng SJC giảm 3,2 triệu đồng/lượng
articles.text:
Giá vàng trong nước hôm nay 27/9/2026
Ngày 26/9, giá vàng miếng SJC được niêm yết ở mức 141,4-144,4 triệu đồng/lượng (mua vào - bán ra), không thay đổi so với phiên liền trước.
Giá vàng nhẫn SJC loại 1-5 chỉ được niêm yết ở mức 140,9-143,9 triệu đồng/lượng (mua vào - bán ra), không thay đổi so với phiên liền trước.
So với cuối tuần trước, giá vàng miếng SJC giảm 3,2 triệu đồng/lượng ở cả chiều mua vào và bán ra. Giá vàng nhẫn SJC loại 1-5 chỉ cũng giảm 3,2 triệu đồng/lượng ở cả chiều mua vào và bán ra so với cuối tuần trước.
Giá vàng nhẫn trơn của Bảo Tín Minh Châu được niêm yết ở mức 141,4-145,4 triệu đồng/lượng (mua vào - bán ra), giảm 100.000 đồng/lượng ở cả chiều mua vào và bán ra so với chốt phiên liền trước.
Giá vàng nhẫn DOJI không thay đổi ở cả hai chiều, giao dịch ở mức 141,5-145,5 triệu đồng/lượng (mua vào - bán ra).
Giá vàng thế giới hôm nay 27/9/2026
Giá vàng thế giới chốt tuần giảm mạnh, chịu sức ép từ lợi suất trái phiếu Mỹ tăng, đồng USD và kỳ vọng Cục Dự trữ Liên bang Mỹ (Fed) tiếp tục duy trì chính sách tiền tệ thắt chặt.
Giá vàng giao ngay đầu tuần ở mức 4.383 USD/ounce. Kim loại quý có thời điểm tăng khi thị trường theo dõi các diễn biến tại Trung Đông và rủi ro liên quan đến eo biển Hormuz. Giá vàng lên mức cao nhất tuần 4.387 USD/ounce, sau đó quay đầu giảm.
Trong hai phiên đầu tuần, giá vàng tiếp tục chịu áp lực. Chứng khoán tăng, lợi suất trái phiếu Mỹ đi lên và đồng USD mạnh hơn khiến nhu cầu đối với vàng giảm. Lo ngại lạm phát khiến thị trường kỳ vọng Fed duy trì chính sách tiền tệ thắt chặt lâu hơn, qua đó gây sức ép lên giá vàng.
Nhà đầu tư quan tâm đến khả năng Fed tăng lãi suất thêm sau khi cơ quan này nâng lãi suất 0,25 điểm phần trăm vào tuần trước. Lãi suất cao làm tăng chi phí cơ hội của việc nắm giữ vàng, tài sản không trả lãi, qua đó thường gây sức ép lên giá kim loại quý.
Áp lực bán tăng mạnh trong phiên thứ Tư và thứ Năm khi lợi suất trái phiếu Mỹ tiếp tục tăng. Giá vàng giao ngay giảm xuống dưới 4.300 USD/ounce và chạm mức thấp nhất tuần 4.244 USD/ounce vào thứ Năm. Lực mua bắt đáy sau đó giúp giá vàng phục hồi.
Phiên cuối tuần, giá vàng được hỗ trợ khi giá dầu hạ nhiệt và xuất hiện kỳ vọng Mỹ - Iran có thể đạt thỏa thuận, qua đó giảm bớt rủi ro gián đoạn nguồn cung năng lượng qua eo biển Hormuz. Đồng USD cũng suy yếu, hỗ trợ giá vàng.
Thị trường vẫn đặt cược vào khả năng Fed tiếp tục tăng lãi suất. Giá vàng giao ngay chưa thể trở lại trên 4.300 USD/ounce. Chốt tuần, giá vàng giao ngay ở mức khoảng 4.286 USD/ounce. Giá vàng kỳ hạn tháng 11/2026 giao dịch quanh mức 4.320 USD/ounce.
Dự báo giá vàng
Barbara Lambrecht, chuyên gia phân tích hàng hóa tại Commerzbank, cho rằng lợi suất trái phiếu Mỹ tăng và kỳ vọng lãi suất cao hơn đang gây sức ép lên giá vàng. Theo bà, điều này làm tăng chi phí cơ hội của việc nắm giữ vàng.
Ngân hàng Đức nhận định giá vàng hiện vẫn cao hơn đáng kể so với hai tháng trước. Khi đó, giá vàng đang ở quanh ngưỡng hỗ trợ 4.000 USD/ounce, trong bối cảnh lợi suất trái phiếu và kỳ vọng lãi suất thấp hơn hiện nay.
Theo Lambrecht, dòng tiền của các nhà đầu tư dài hạn vẫn duy trì tại các quỹ ETF vàng. Dòng tiền này có thể góp phần hạn chế áp lực điều chỉnh đối với giá vàng.
Neil Welsh, Trưởng bộ phận kim loại tại Britannia Global Markets, cho rằng thị trường vàng vẫn có những yếu tố hỗ trợ về dài hạn. Nhu cầu mua vàng của các ngân hàng trung ương vẫn cao. Căng thẳng địa chính trị kéo dài và những lo ngại về tình hình tài khóa cũng tiếp tục hỗ trợ kim loại quý.
Joy Yang, Giám đốc toàn cầu về quản lý sản phẩm chỉ số tại MarketVector Indexes, nhận định vàng còn được hưởng lợi từ việc thị trường chứng khoán biến động thấp. Chỉ số S&P 500 vẫn duy trì gần mức cao kỷ lục trên 7.000 điểm, dù lạm phát tăng và lợi suất trái phiếu ở mức cao.
Theo Yang, một bộ phận nhà đầu tư chứng khoán có thể đang sử dụng vàng như một công cụ phòng vệ trước những rủi ro trên thị trường trái phiếu. Dòng tiền này có thể tiếp tục hỗ trợ giá vàng nếu áp lực lạm phát giảm.

articles.title: How powerful of a power bank do you need to safely charge a laptop? - Engadget
articles.text:
How powerful of a power bank do you need to safely charge a laptop?
Don’t let the big mAh number fool you. The better comparison is watt-hours.
While most good power banks can theoretically extend your laptop's runtime by providing a small amount of charge, a proper laptop power bank will store enough energy and charge faster than the battery drains. Two values explain the experience you'll have: watt-hours (Wh) for capacity and watts (W) for output. Power banks provide their capacities in milliamp-hours (mAh), but for a proper measure of capacity across devices (especially for a higher-drain device like a laptop), you need to multiply this value by the voltage to get the true amount of energy stored in watt-hours.
Most power banks store energy in lithium-ion cells at about 3.7 volts (V). Watts are equal to volts times amperes, and you must divide the mAh count by 1,000 since 1,000 mAh is one amp. So for example, a 10,000 mAh bank stores roughly 37Wh (3.7V x 10Ah) before conversion loss. Doubling the mAh doubles the Wh as long as voltage stays consistent, so a 20,000 mAh bank is about 74Wh.
Next, you need to know the Wh rating of your laptop's battery, which you should be able to find on the manufacturer's website. Without a wattmeter, it's difficult to know how much power your laptop uses on average, so we can estimate it by dividing the Wh capacity by how many hours the battery lasts. For example, a 70Wh battery that runs for 5 hours is averaging 14W of power usage. Of course, the instantaneous power usage differs based on what you're doing (scrolling a PDF uses far less energy than rendering video).
Using modern MacBooks as an illustration, their batteries are rated from ~37Wh (MacBook Neo) up to 100Wh (16-inch MacBook Pro). That means charging your MacBook with a 10,000 mAh (37Wh) bank won't even provide a full top-up in most cases. And the capacity doesn't tell you how fast the charging happens.
Understanding what your power bank is capable of
Before you calculate how long a power bank should run your laptop for, you also must take into account that the charging process isn't perfectly efficient. For fast charging standards like USB Power Delivery, the bank has to increase its voltage to push enough power (watts) to charge your laptop quickly enough that it doesn't drain. Some energy is lost in this changeover, as well as generally from heat. 20 percent efficiency loss is a general rule for normal charging, but around 30 percent (or even higher) is more realistic when fast charging.
With all these values, you can finally estimate how much additional time a power bank will run your laptop for. Say you connect a 20,000 mAh 45W USB-C bank to the theoretical laptop mentioned above. Subtracting 30 percent for the overhead, that 74Wh power bank has an effective capacity of ~52Wh. With a laptop averaging 14W, the power bank would extend its runtime by around 3.7 hours. If the laptop ever needs to draw more than the 45W the bank can provide, it will draw power from its internal battery alongside it — the bank is thus supplementing the internal battery to extend its life.
The important point is that you can't assume a power bank's capacity is the same as its output. A portable 50,000 mAh battery is great, but that capacity doesn't tell you how much power it pushes. A large-capacity bank rated at 15W will only slow the laptop's power drain, or it could be rejected entirely. For laptop banks, the label to look for is "USB-C PD." In simple language, this means the bank and laptop negotiate a higher charging level than an ordinary USB port.
Always check the bank's per-port output too, because the total output number can be deceptive. For instance, if the bank description says "100W total," it may not be capable of this full output on any given port, or it may deliver less than 100W when you're charging a phone and a laptop at the same time.
For most people, a 20,000 mAh/74Wh bank is a reasonable emergency or partial-charge option, while a 27,000 mAh/100Wh is closer to the sweet spot. In the US, 100Wh is also the limit for power banks allowed on a plane without approval. if you need suggestions, our favorite laptop power banks span all needs.
Why can't my power bank charge my laptop?
Similarly to plugging your laptop into your car's USB port, a weak power bank might be providing power to your laptop, but not as fast as the laptop's battery is draining under use. There are a few other possibilities. Check whether your laptop supports charging through USB-C. Some USB-C ports handle data, video or other accessories, but can't run a charger. If there's no indication on the ports themselves, check the manual if you still have it or look at the product specs online.
Next, check whether the bank supports USB-C Power Delivery at a high enough per-port wattage. A basic 15W USB-C output can charge a phone, but won't make a dent in a laptop drawing 65W+. If the bank's output is below the laptop's needs, the computer will either reject it or only charge under light use after warning you of a "slow charge."
Lastly, check the cable, as not every USB-C cable is rated to carry high-wattage power. A standard USB-C cable generally supports up to 3 amps, while higher-power 100W and Extended Power Range connections will require a 5-amp-rated cable. USB PD 3.1 can provide up to 240W, but only when the laptop, bank and cable all support the needed power level.
As long as the hardware is compliant, your USB-C PD devices will negotiate a compatible voltage and current. Avoid anything that's damaged or ancient cables you hauled out of a cardboard box — those aren't going to handle today's power needs.

articles.title: Discord rolls out global age checks for all users
articles.text:
Discord has started a global rollout of age checks that place users into age groups, with extra safety settings for teenagers. The rollout began on 22 September and will take several days, the company said in a blog post by chief technology officer Stanislav Vishnevskiy.
TNW is owned by Tekpon. Discord is listed on Tekpon’s marketplace.
Every account is put into one of three groups: adult, teen (13 to 17) or unconfirmed. Discord said more than 90% of users will be sorted automatically and will not need to prove their age.
To do this, the company uses a model that looks at account signals, such as how old the account is, which servers it joins and how active it is. Discord said the model does not read messages, calls or other content.
Users the model cannot place, or who want to confirm they are adults, can use other methods. These include a credit card check, age-range sharing from Apple’s App Store or Google Play, and a Google Wallet ID. Users can also take a video selfie processed on the device, scan an ID, or use a reusable credential called AgeKey.
Discord said its partners return only an age group and delete the data they receive. It also said it no longer uses manual reviews of ID documents, after a 2025 breach at a former support vendor.
For teen accounts, messages from people who are not friends go to a separate requests inbox. Age-restricted servers and channels are blocked, and sensitive images are blurred. Teens’ full profiles are visible only to friends and members of smaller servers.
Adults will see no change, according to the company. Users who have already confirmed their age do not need to do it again.
The age estimation model is not being used in the UK and Australia, where Discord already runs separate systems to meet local rules. It first expanded age checks in Texas and Brazil after those places brought in their own requirements.
Discord first announced global teen-by-default settings in February, with a rollout planned for March. It later delayed the launch to the second half of 2026 to add more ways to verify age.

articles.title: Googlebooks might be the real deal
articles.text:
Hi, friends! Welcome to Installer No. 145, your guide to the best and Verge-iest stuff in the world. (If you’re new here, welcome, I’m happy to be done traveling for a bit, and also you can read all the old editions at the Installer homepage.)
Googlebooks might be the real deal
Plus, in this week’s Installer: New Meta glasses, Remedy’s Control sequel, Microsoft’s updated Surface Mouse, and more.
This week, I flew to San Francisco to try out Meta’s new hardware, including the impressive Meta VR Glasses. Along the way, I’ve been listening to Joanna Stern’s interview with Mark Zuckerberg, watching this interview with new Apple CEO John Ternus, revisiting Steve Jobs’ “Antennagate” press conference Q&A, playing games on my Steam Deck using the Xreal One Pro glasses, and reading Sarah Wynn-Williams’ Careless People when I have spare moments.
I also have for you more on Meta’s glasses, Remedy’s Control sequel, Microsoft’s updated Surface Mouse, and more.
(As always, the best part of Installer is your ideas and tips. What apps are you into right now? What are your favorite things you’ve watched / seen / listened to recently? Tell me everything: installer@theverge.com. And if you know someone else who might enjoy Installer, forward it to them and tell them to subscribe here.)
The Drop
- Google’s Googlebooks. Google finally revealed a ton of details about its Googlebook laptops, and they seem like they could be particularly great for people looking for a laptop to pair with their Android phone. Google is promising that they’ll get 10 years of updates, which hopefully speaks to a real commitment from the company to make the platform work. The first five are from Acer, Asus, Dell, HP, and Lenovo.
- Ray-Ban Meta Audio. Meta is launching smart glasses without cameras. The glasses still have microphones and speakers, so you can still listen to music and talk with AI. Battery life is longer, and there are also some new styles. Not going to lie, I really like the Clubmaster style.
- Control Resonant. Remedy’s Control sequel moves out of the mind-bending Oldest House and into Manhattan and some strange new locations. I’ve beaten it, and while I prefer the original’s more contained setting, I love a lot about where the story goes. If you’re a Remedy fan, don’t miss this one.
- Silent Hill: Townfall. Reviews for Konami’s next big horror game, set in a town in Scotland, make it sound like another worthy addition to the franchise. It should be a great one to check out to get ready for Halloween.
- Peloton’s Tread Flex. Peloton made a folding treadmill. (Folding is all the rage these days.) Seems like a smart idea, especially for Peloton faithfuls who have smaller living spaces. It’s also Peloton’s “most affordable” treadmill, though it still costs $2,195.
- Microsoft’s Surface Mouse. The second-generation version of the Surface Mouse has haptic feedback, an action button, and can be paired with three devices. It’s a tad pricey at $79.99, but it seems like a really solid option if you just want a good mouse. The Surface Pro and Laptop got a refresh, too.
- Logitech G’s Yeti 2. The follow-up to the Blue Yeti, one of the most recognizable microphones ever, has an LED display and can track your voice with an audio proximity sensor. I just picked up a cheap mic of my own on a Whoop sale, but maybe if that one doesn’t cut it, I’ll end up snagging a Yeti 2.
Today I’m featuring The Verge’s Brad Bourque. Brad joined our commerce team for a few months to help out with our deals coverage and has been going deep into gaming tech. He’s also a fellow Portlander, so I had to feature him as one of our small but mighty Portland contingent.
I asked Brad to share his homescreen and the apps and things he cares about. Here it is, plus some info on the apps he uses and why:
The phone: Pixel 9 Pro XL
The wallpaper: My homescreen wallpaper is just an included Pixel wallpaper of plants in mellow green tones. My lockscreen is a fan-made Tekken Tag Tournament poster featuring Armor King and Modelo. It doesn’t have to make sense if the vibes are right.
The apps:
- Right up top you’ll find two of my favorite mobile games. The first is Idle Obelisk Miner, an idle game I recently started playing that I’ve found compelling and generous given the genre’s normal conditions. I’ve been playing for just over a month and a half and I’m only at 3.16 percent completion, so I know I have a long road ahead of me.
- The other is Nubby’s Number Factory, an oddball roguelike that I’ve sunk dozens of hours into on Steam. The game has a funky style and charm that reminds me of old Adobe Flash browser games, but with modern sensibilities and huge replayability.
- Other than that, there isn’t much exciting to discuss. I like to keep calendar and weather widgets prominently featured on my first screen, mostly because I’m bad at remembering what I have coming up on any given day and Portland is known for surprise rainstorms.
- The main screen is mostly the boring stuff that I use every day, with apps like mail, texting, and YouTube given priority positions for easy access. My dark secret is that, if you swipe one page to the right, it’s all a disorganized mess of apps with no sorting or folders. If I’m looking for a specific app, I’ll swipe up and search for it.
I also asked Brad to share a few things he’s into right now. Here’s what he sent back:
- Ever since the final major Destiny 2 update, I’ve been chiseling away at some of the expansions I missed and finishing up old collections. With the recent announcement that old vaulted content would be coming back, I’m planning on continuing to sink time into one of my favorite games ever.
- The other game I’ve been playing quite a lot of over the past few months is Old School RuneScape. I didn’t play during its heyday, so I don’t actually have much nostalgia for the game, but I’ve been really sucked in by how different it is from other MMOs that I’ve been playing for years, like World of Warcraft. I also appreciate that direct user feedback is such a big part of modernizing and updating the game, which I think has helped foster an active and social community in-game.
- We’re at the end of Game Changer’s latest season. It’s Dropout TV’s groundbreaking game show where the rules change every time, so I’m watching that religiously on Monday evenings. The most recent season has been one of the strongest yet, and constantly has me laughing and occasionally crying over its sweet and incredibly creative episodes.
- For music, I’ve been on a really chill kick lately, with Janelle Monáe’s The Age of Pleasure and Tom Misch’s Full Circle headlining a lot of my morning writing and deal-hunting sessions. I’ve been listening to a lot of vinyl recently, which I’ve found gives a nice rhythm and ritual to my day that just turning on Spotify and hitting shuffle doesn’t.
Crowdsourced
Here’s what the Installer community is into this week. I want to know what you’re into right now as well! Email installer@theverge.com with your recommendations for anything and everything, and we’ll feature some of our favorites here every week. For even more great recommendations, check out the replies to this post on The Verge.
“I’ve been really enjoying a new app for my self-hosted media server. NostalgiaTV uses your media library to set up TV channels akin to classic cable. You turn it on and it brings up the ‘live’ TV guide/schedule and you can channel surf to choose what to watch instead of scrolling through your media library. Totally unnecessary and also way more fun than I thought it would be. They automatically set up a few channels for you, but you can also get in the weeds setting up custom channels and schedules.” — vikrael
“Currently playing: Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave, only during the evenings when my son is put to sleep. Reading: The Iliad, I try to read it in bits whenever I can during the early part of the evening during the week. I read more during the weekend mornings.” — basicalexguy
“As a fan of the Planet Money podcast, I was surprised to come across their new book at my local library. Now being a few chapters into it, I am pleasantly surprised about how good of a read it is (especially if you enjoy the podcast). Title is Planet Money: A Guide to the Economic Forces That Shape Your Life.” — YG_400
“Currently reading The God of the Woods by Liz Moore that is being adapted into a Netflix show soon. The book is so good and hard to put down as the mystery draws you in as you hope for answers with each turn of the page.” — Sabertooth
“In the final act of Star Wars Zero Company. It is VERY good.” — BV
“I just recently got back into photography after years of just shooting on my iPhone and trying to tweak the results. Wow have I missed my Ricoh GRIII and Olympus XA2. While the Ricoh gives me instant gratification of capturing a moment exactly how I envisioned it, it’s been a lot of fun shooting rolls of film (stored in the freezer of course), and having to patiently wait for the results to come back!” — Ricky
Signing off
Well, after my big tip in this section last week about eating at familiar restaurants while traveling, I wasn’t able to do any of that while traveling for Meta, and I felt it. Boy was I tired and hungry. It came down to a few different things, like a busier schedule and mostly being on Meta’s campus, where eating options were limited. I did get to devour some protein bars, which are a guilty pleasure of mine. But I really was hankering for some Chipotle.
See you next week!

articles.title: I Took an At-Home Pet DNA Test Kit and Found Out My Cat Is a Cat
articles.text:
An at-home cat or dog DNA test kit promises to give pet owners clarity on a heap of important health data, like breed ancestry, blood type, and health risks. To access this info, owners just swab the inside of their pet’s mouth, seal the sample in a prepaid-postage envelope, and wait (for up to five weeks) for results to be sent to their inbox. Each company has a testing lab, and the results live in your online account, where they can be downloaded and even shared with your vet.
But because of several factors, such as sample size and comparison, these tests often give dramatically different results for things like genetic ancestry and breed traits (more on that below).
I tested several at-home DNA test kits, including two of the most popular kits—Basepaws ($104) and Wisdom Panel ($97)—on my two adult cats and talked to several animal experts to get insights into these tests—and whether they are worth your money, given the large disparity in results. Think of this as the WIRED guide to the increasingly popular at-home pet DNA test.
Table of Contents
Be sure to check out our related guides, like the Best Automatic Cat Feeders, Best Automatic Litter Boxes, Best Automatic Cat Fountains, and Best Dog Accessories.
Love WIRED? Add us as a preferred source on Google to see more of us.
Easiest Interface
|  | Breed | Health Test | Trait Test | Blood Type/Transfusion Risk | Oral Health Report | Family Tree | 
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Wisdom Panel (Cat) | Screens for 70+ breeds and populations | Tests for 45+ genetic health conditions | Test for 25+ physical traits | Yes | No | Yes | 
In my research, I've found that people widely consider Wisdom Panel the most trusted at-home pet DNA test kit (along with dog-only Embark, which former WIRED reviewer Julia Forbes tested below).
Wisdom Panel offers several kits for dogs (listed below) but only one test for cats. It can identify more than 70 breeds, includes 45 health tests, determines blood type, and screens for more than 25 traits. It even provides a genetic consult for “at-risk” health findings and shows what the pet's family tree might look like based on DNA results. I especially liked that it tests for the most common conditions seen in cats or dogs with a similar breed makeup to your pet (based on the DNA sample), including important markers like drug sensitivity, immune deficiency, and bleeding disorders. It also identified the cat’s blood type (both of my cats were A) and transfusion risk (both were moderate).
The results arrived live online in my Wisdom Panel account within three weeks of mailing them. I really appreciated the interface, which was organized into clickable tabs that made the information easier to access and navigate. Plus, based on appearance alone, my cat Clover's DNA results seemed most accurate with this test (below). I also tested my run-of-the-mill gray tabby cat, Basil, but on all tests—including Wisdom Panel—he was almost entirely labeled as an “American domestic cat” and “polycat/domestic shorthair." That's basically the mutt final boss, a result of many generations of mixed breeding among different cat types, where ancestry and origin are almost impossible to determine.
| Clover’s Wisdom Panel Results | 
|---|
| American domestic cat: 51 percent | 
| Highlander: 13 percent | 
| Norwegian Forest Cat: 13 percent | 
| Siamese and Oriental: 13 percent | 
| LaPerm: 10 percent | 
Most In-Depth Results
|  | Breed | Health Test | Trait Test | Blood Type/Transfusion Risk | Oral Health Report | Family Tree | 
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Basepaws (Cat) | Tests against 21 breeds | Tests for 64 genetic health markers | Tests for 50 genetic trait markers | Yes | Yes | No | 
WIRED reviewed Basepaws over half a decade ago, and a lot has changed since then. Basepaws offers a single breed and health test for cats that identifies up to 21 breeds, 64 genetic health markers, 50 genetic trait markers, blood type, and oral health. The wait time for results is five weeks, and when I first sent my cat Basil's test in, they couldn't extract enough DNA, so I had to send another sample and wait another five weeks. Rather than an easily digestible interactive screen with information like Wisdom Panel, Basepaws gives you essentially a mini book PDF to scroll through to find information. It feels more in-depth than Wisdom Panel, but it is also harder to disseminate the large pile of information.
Basepaws tests genes for markers associated with disorders in musculoskeletal and connective tissue; eyes; metabolic, autoimmune, and endocrine systems; blood; and more. Both of my cats, Clover and Basil, were cleared of any genes that would mark them as potential carriers of genetic diseases. It also identified blood type and transfusion risk, which were A and moderate (the same results I got with Wisdom Panel’s test).
Basepaws tests for oral health by comparing against an oral microbiome database. In this regard, Basepaws wins out. Dental health is a major concern for me, and I love that Basepaws screens for it and provides an oral health report (I have since started brushing my cats' teeth). My cat Basil was at high risk for all dental markers like halitosis, tooth resorption, and periodontal disease. Basepaws developed a health plan for him: “Adopt a daily oral health care routine, consider supplementing Basil’s routine with products accepted by the Veterinary Oral Health Council, and schedule an appointment with your veterinarian in the next month.” Although I was alarmed by the results, I appreciated that Basepaws provided recommended next steps so I could develop a plan of action for care. And it’s important to remember that these results don’t necessarily mean a pet is guaranteed to develop the disease.
"These can be a helpful flag for your veterinarian to keep an eye on [...] but do not necessarily mean aggressive testing is needed at that moment,” says Jamie Richardson, head of veterinary medicine at Small Door Veterinary. “DNA tests are tools to support—not replace—veterinary care.”
Some of the other Basepaws results, particularly the genetic and physical markers, seem off. Like Wisdom Panel, white calico Clover was marked as “likely” to be black in color, and none of the ancestral DNA breeds matched across tests for Clover.
| Clover’s Basepaws Results | 
|---|
| Polycat (domestic shorthair): 20.61 percent | 
| Broadly Western: 16.91 percent | 
| American Shorthair: 14.45 percent | 
| Maine coon: 12.27 percent | 
| Ragdoll: 11.8 percent | 
| Persian: 6.99 percent | 
| Siberian: 6.2 percent | 
| Abyssinian: 5.62 percent | 
| Burmese: 3.07 percent | 
| Savannah: 2.08 percent | 
Another Cat DNA Test Kit I Tested
|  | Breed | Health Test | Trait Test | Blood Type/Transfusion Risk | Oral Health Report | Family Tree | 
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Koko Genetics | Yes; tests against an unspecified number | Tests for 55 genetic health markers | Tests for 40 traits | No | No | Yes | 
Koko Genetics was a new name to me, but it offers a similar service to the two major brands above, with tests for both cats and dogs in “starter” basic and “advanced” kits. I tested the latter, which provides additional health insights by screening for genetic disorders or abnormalities. The process is exactly the same as with the other kits, where you swab your cat's mouth, register your kit online, and mail the results. The Koko Genetics interface wouldn't allow me to register two kits with different cats under the same login/username, so I had to create two separate accounts with two different emails, which was a slight pain. The results also took surprisingly long—it took over five weeks from mailing to being acknowledged as received, and an additional five weeks to get results.
This interface was the least user-friendly of all I tested, and many of the default options were in Spanish with no English options. The site where you access results is a little bare-bones, with additional information available if you click the tab. I found that much of the health trait info was scientific jargon, and I had to do further research to understand it. Clover was flagged as having a copy of the Acute Intermittent Porphyria (Variant 3) gene mutation, which can cause discolored teeth and urine and may lead to other health problems. Luckily, Clover has just one copy of the mutation and will not develop the disease, but she can transmit the mutation to her offspring. (She's spayed, so that is not a potential issue.) Wisdom Panel also tests for this, and she was not flagged as carrying it in that test.
Both cats were negative for all physical traits except black coat (which neither has), and I didn't find the info really helpful or interesting. There's also a family tree option, like Wisdom Panel's, where you can see what the previous generations' breed or coloring might've been.
| Clover’s Koko Genetics Results | 
|---|
| Domestic cat: 59.5 percent | 
| Sphynx: 8.8 percent | 
| Turkish Van: 6.6 percent | 
| Maine Coon: 6.3 percent | 
| LaPerm: 5.7 percent | 
| Munchkin cat: 4.6 percent | 
| Norwegian Forest Cat: 4.4 percent | 
| Chartreux: 4.1 percent | 
Best Dog DNA Test Kit
|  | Breed | Health Test | Trait Test | Blood Type/Transfusion Risk | Oral Health Report | Family Tree | 
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Embark Dog | Tests against over 400 breeds | No | No; results for likely personality traits rather than physical | No | No | Yes | 
One of my family’s favorite pastimes is placing low-stakes bets on the breeds that make up our beloved rescue dogs. Usually we’re wildly off with our estimates. For my dog Randy, all we knew was that he was a Chihuahua mix. The Embark DNA kit is the dog equivalent of Ancestry DNA for humans, given how detailed it is. The test kit uses a saliva sample, and you ship it off for processing. Within three weeks, we found out Randy had quite the cocker spaniel lineage, with show-dog cousins across the country (Princess Elysia of Eagle’s Wings’ parents, if you’re reading this, hello!).
The Embark app gives detailed breakdowns of behavioral, health, and longevity insights for the breeds that make up your pup. His personality analysis shows he’s closely aligned with his cocker spaniel roots, always on the lookout (check), sometimes high-energy (check), and rarely independent (spot on). —Julia Forbes
The kits below are also specifically for dogs from Basepaws and Wisdom Panel, two companies I've tested on my cats.
How Does a DNA Test Kit Work?
Pet DNA tests rely on pet owners collecting cells via a cheek swab, then placing the sample in a sealed stabilizing or preserving fluid for transit. You’ll mail the sample back to the lab in the prepaid envelope. It usually takes about five weeks to get results. (The first time I sent my cat Basil’s Basepaws sample, the company emailed that the results were inconclusive, and I had to wait for another kit to be sent, re-swab him, and wait another five weeks for results.)
At the lab, the sample is analyzed against the company’s breed and genetic health database. They use single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) arrays—the standard technology for identifying breed ancestry—as well as data on inherited traits and the risk of common diseases. Essentially, different breeds have distinct patterns of SNPs in their genomes, which serve as genetic markers. These tests analyze the pet’s DNA sample for specific SNPs and then compare them to the company’s existing database to estimate the animal’s breed composition. This not only tells you about breed composition, but can also identify the specific DNA sequences that are markers for potential health risks, such as predispositions to diseases or hereditary cancers.
Don’t take the health or DNA test results as absolute truth, however. “This can lead to a false sense of security or false alarms," says veterinarian Amanda Chambers. Forward your results to your veterinarian and always follow up by scheduling a visit to the vet if your pet is marked as a carrier for any genetic disease.
What the Results Can—and Can’t—Tell You
After chatting with Richardson, I’ve found that these are the major areas of limitation with at-home DNA test kits:
- Results depend on the size/diversity of the genetic database
- Most kits test known markers only—not full genomes
- Feline data is less developed
- Misinterpretation of results can lead to unnecessary concern
Wisdom Panel claims its cat breed results are over 98 percent accurate and its dog tests are over 99 percent accurate. However, there's a huge disparity between the three kits I tested on my cats, particularly in breed ancestry. One problem with the vast disparity in results is that the three companies use different sample sizes and metrics to identify breeds.
But the biggest issue for cat owners taking these at-home DNA tests is that you can’t really identify most cats' breeds the way you can with dogs. Unless your cat is a purebred, about 95 percent of cats don’t belong to a recognized breed. Cats' genetic backgrounds are muddied—they're just similar mixes with different physical characteristics, so the tests only show the breed(s) they share the most markers with. Basically, these tests for cats aren’t able to reliably tell us about breed composition, just similarity to other breeds’ traits in the company’s data pool.
From my research, it seems the breed identification part of these tests is more accurate for dogs, as dog DNA is so much more diversified. Breeds have been clearly defined after centuries of diversification, and dog DNA mutates quickly, with genes changing after just a few generations. Cats are not much different from their Egyptian ancestors.
Interestingly, in a 2023 CBS report, the news organization sent dog and human DNA to different at-home test companies and received varying results, with the dog's DNA ranging from 65 to only 29 percent German Shepherd. The human DNA results were attributed to a bulldog, border collie, and cane corso mix.
In summation, unfortunately, there isn't a single catchall way to determine a pet's genetic makeup or ancestry. Humans like categories, and breeds are essentially human constructs based on how a dog or cat looks. The genetic part of the test is fun, but take it with a grain of salt—especially with cats.
A Note on At-Home Allergy Testing Kits
I recently tested both of my cats for allergies and intolerances using a similar at-home test kit, the 5Strands Pet Food & Environmental Intolerance Test, for $100. For this, you only need to send a fur sample in the mail to a lab; results were sent to my inbox within seven days. The report showed that both of my cats had strong intolerances to common ingredients in their diet, such as various types of fish and chicken meal. This sent me into a panic about my cats' health and (dis)comfort.
After further research, I learned that hair/fur samples are not an accurate way to measure allergies and intolerances. Studies show that kits claiming to provide these results perform no better than chance and often produce inconsistent or false results.
“There's no scientific evidence to support allergy testing through hair, fur, or saliva,” says Richardson. “Veterinarian-supervised elimination diets to test for food allergy and intradermal skin testing or blood tests to test for environmental allergies remain the gold standard.”
So, save your money and consult a vet instead if you suspect your pet is suffering from allergies or intolerances.
Meet the Experts
- Amanda Chambers is a full-time small animal general practitioner based in Kansas City, Missouri.
- Jamie Richardson is head of veterinary medicine at Small Door Veterinary.

articles.title: Why measuring B2B marketing by leads fails
articles.text:
B2B companies today can track almost every movement a prospect makes, yet the numbers that appear most prominently on dashboards can still have little connection to the number executives and stakeholders ultimately care about: revenue. 87% of B2B marketers found it increasingly difficult to measure the long-term impact of campaigns, while nearly half were required to justify marketing spend to CFOs and CEOs every month.
This pressure is intensifying as software buyers take increasingly complicated routes to purchase. Gartner found in 2026 that B2B buyers use an average of seven information sources during a purchase, with 45% turning to generative AI during their research. At the same time, 67% preferred a completely digital, sales rep-free buying experience. A click therefore marks an increasingly small moment in a much larger commercial journey.
Yet marketing reporting can still end at the first conversion. A campaign generates leads, and the cost per lead looks acceptable, yet the harder question comes later: did those prospects enter a qualified pipeline, did they become customers, and did the advertising spend produce an economic return? Often, there’s a disconnect between what B2B marketing teams are trying to accomplish and what they measure, with lead-based metrics remaining widely used even as companies pursue account-based growth.
The problem becomes sharper in software markets, where a purchase can involve several stakeholders and repeated research before a deal closes. Gartner found that 74% of B2B buying teams experienced unhealthy conflict during the decision process, while buying groups can span five to 16 people. Attribution, under those conditions, is less a reporting exercise than an attempt to reconstruct how a commercial decision actually happened.
It is this gap that Waqas Khokhar, founder and CEO of ScalixAI, has made pivotal to his thinking. Khokhar, who spent nine years at Google before building the company, approaches paid advertising through the lens of the business outcome it is meant to influence. His argument lies in the belief that marketing should ultimately be accountable for the commercial journey it helps create.
Khokhar believes the difficulty starts with attribution itself. “The biggest issue is that companies don’t understand how individual channels influence the end goal, which is revenue,” he explains. In a product-led business, that means understanding how far a customer travels after arriving. In a sales-led model, he argues, obsessing over the cost of a booked demo can obscure whether those demos are producing commercially viable opportunities.
His experience at Google also shaped his view of how paid search should be managed. “Google Ads is ever-changing and ever-evolving, and most people don’t know how to move with the way the algorithm moves,” Khokhar argues. His analogy is a boat in a storm: fighting the current with a fixed playbook makes little sense when the environment itself keeps changing.
The more consequential shift, however, is what happens after the click. Khokhar states, “We want to know: what did I invest, and what did I get out of it?” CAC and CPA still have a role in establishing healthy economics, he argues, but pipeline and closed revenue provide the harder test.
ScalixAI’s reported client outcomes are used to illustrate that philosophy. Khokhar points to Oneleet, which generated 660 demos alongside more than $1 million in closed revenue and more than $2 million in active pipeline. Fyxer, he points out, reached more than 10,000 customers while recording 20x revenue growth within a year, while PAM AI delivered more than 3x ROI within months. These figures form the evidence behind the company’s argument that advertising needs to be evaluated inside the wider revenue system.
Khokhar puts the philosophy in more human terms. He observes that the company’s core values emerged through working with clients instead of being selected as abstract corporate principles. Referrals have since become its main sales channel, he notes, with client recommendations providing evidence that the partnership model is carrying weight commercially.
That model also shapes how ScalixAI charges. The company uses a flat retainer, a structure Khokhar frames as a reflection of where the agency believes its interests should sit: with the client’s growth rather than with the size of the media budget. Khokhar similarly argues that an agency should function as an extension of its client’s team, with regular communication and a genuine understanding of the business.
The operational challenge now is scale. Khokhar highlights that ScalixAI moved from zero to roughly 30 clients in 14 months, with selectivity playing a large role in protecting the company’s culture. He recalls terminating one relationship only days after it began because the working expectations were fundamentally misaligned. “Protecting the team’s energy is part of the job,” he argues.
His next target is growing clientele, supported by the systems and processes he began building early in the company’s growth. The larger question, though, reaches well beyond one agency. As B2B buyers move across search, social, AI, and human validation, marketers face a growing demand to prove what their activity actually produces.
